registration, from an enrolment codeFor the user the code was issued for, sent from the link or from a recovery code typed in. The code is held against the challenge, not spent.Records the passkey, spends the code, and signs its user in with a full session.
registration, from a sessionFor the session's user, who adds a passkey on the enrolment page once signed in, a session that may only enrol included, and asked of a session signed in to within the last 10 minutes. A bearer token registers nothing, the bootstrap token's included, since a passkey is registered in a browser.Records the passkey, held to the same 10 minutes from when its options were issued, and opens no other session: its user is signed in already.
  • A challenge is 32 random bytes, single use and good for 5 minutes, the time a person takes to find an authenticator and unlock it, and kept in the database, so that the options and the verification may reach two replicas of the API. The verification takes it whatever follows, so that no answer is replayed.
  • A registration asks for a discoverable credential, so that signing in needs no login typed first, and excludes the passkeys the user holds, so that an authenticator makes no second one for the same account. Its label, optional, is at most 256 characters on one line.
  • Both routes answer 403 to a request whose Origin header is not the public URL's origin: the page asks with fetch, which sends it, and a form posted from another page, or from a sandboxed frame writing Origin: null, would otherwise sign a browser in as whoever that page's author chose. On an installation addressed by an IP address both answer 409, saying why.
  • A sign-in or a registration refused is one 401 sentence whatever the reason, so that a failure teaches nothing about which part was wrong; a synced passkey where device_bound_only applies is a 403 naming the setting, since its holder can do something about it.
PageDoes
/auth/sign-inSigns in with a passkey, or a password where the policy offers one; says who the browser is signed in as, or that its session may only enrol, and offers to sign out of either, since whoever next uses a shared machine could otherwise enrol a passkey of their own on the account; and lists what a signed-in account signs in with, removes one, and sets a password and a TOTP generator where the policy allows passwords.
/auth/enrolEnrols a passkey, or sets a password where the policy allows passwords, with the code of an enrolment link or a recovery code typed in, or, in a signed-in browser, adds a passkey to the session's user; then offers to enrol another, on another device, so that losing one is an inconvenience rather than an incident.

Every answer of the page carries a Content-Security-Policy letting it load its own stylesheet and three scripts and reach its own origin, and nothing else: no script or style written into it, no form posted, never framed. It sends no Referer, since its address may carry agk login's challenge, and every request it makes is a fetch in the default mode, since a browser writes Origin: null on a form posted from such a page, which the API refuses. The HTML is never cached and the files are revalidated at every load, so that an upgrade never serves a page beside another release's scripts, and its links are relative, so that it works where the public URL has a path.

A browser runs the ceremony only on a page whose certificate it trusts, never one clicked past a warning: the certificate init issues is trusted on the machine that signs in, as From another machine does for agk, or a reverse proxy serves one of its own.

Signing in from a terminal

  1. agk login listens on a port of the loopback, makes a one-time verifier and opens the browser at the sign-in page, handing it the loopback address and the verifier's SHA-256.
  2. The person signs in in the browser, with a passkey against the same Relying Party as every other sign-in, or a password where the policy allows one: the only way on an installation addressed by an IP address.
  3. The page redirects to the loopback address with a one-time code: single use, good for a minute.
  4. agk sends the code and the verifier to POST /api/v1/auth/exchange and is answered an API token, which it stores in the local profile.

The exchange is PKCE's (RFC 7636): a code seen on the way, in the browser's history or by another process on the machine, opens nothing without the verifier, which never left agk. A device code, the other common way to sign in a terminal, can be phished, since anybody can send someone a code to approve for them. A machine with no browser takes a token made elsewhere, in AGENTIIK_TOKEN.

The code is bound to the challenge, the account and the credential that signed in, and spent by the first exchange its schema accepts, whatever verifier it carries, so that whoever saw it on the way cannot try again. It opens nothing once its account is suspended or removed, or its credential removed, or its password set anew. A sign-in whose session may only enrol hands agk no code, and a code mints what the session beside it may do when it is traded: none where the policy has since come to require a passkey, to forbid passwords, or to refuse a synced passkey with device_bound_only. The loopback address, 127.0.0.1 or [::1] by number and never localhost, takes one request, a navigation to the address agk gave the page: a browser on another machine, over SSH for instance, reaches it through a forwarded port, ssh -N -L PORT:127.0.0.1:PORT host, which agk login prints. The challenge is no secret, so somebody else on the same machine could bring agk a code of their own sign-in; agk says who it signed in as.

Verifying a passkey

From v0.3.0, the API verifies registrations and assertions with the Go standard library alone: a CBOR decoder written for it and fuzzed; COSE keys ES256, EdDSA and RS256, offered in that order and checked with crypto/ecdsa, crypto/ed25519 and crypto/rsa; attestation conveyance none, the attestation format none accepted.

InRefused
CBORAn indefinite length, a map key written twice, a byte after the item, a head longer than its value needs, a tag, a float, null or undefined; more than 5 levels of nesting, 256 items or 16 KiB. One value has one encoding, since two encodings are where two parsers start to disagree about what a credential says.
client dataAnother type, challenge or origin than the ceremony's; a member written twice, or text that is not UTF-8; a ceremony run in a frame, crossOrigin true or a topOrigin present, since the sign-in page is never framed.
authenticator dataAnother Relying Party than the installation's; a user not present, at every ceremony, since the API creates no credential without the user's gesture; a user not verified where user_verification is required; a passkey backed up but not eligible for backup; a byte past what the data describes; a credential ID empty or over 1,023 bytes.
attestationAny format but none, a packed self attestation included: it proves only that the new key signed, which the first assertion proves anyway.
an ES256 keyA point not on P-256, or one written compressed.
an EdDSA keyA point not on Ed25519 or not in its canonical form, and the eight points of small order, against which a signature made with no private key verifies for any message.
an RS256 keyA modulus under 2,048 bits, over 8,192 or even; an exponent even, under 3 or past 31 bits; either written with a leading zero byte. 2,048 bits is the smallest still held secure, and 8,192, twice the largest in common use, bounds what one assertion costs the server with a key its holder chose.
an assertionA Backup Eligibility other than the one registered, and a signature counter that did not move forward.

A passkey's signature counter moves forward at every assertion, or stays at zero where the authenticator keeps none, as the synced passkeys most people hold do; two zeros are accepted. A counter at or below the stored one, one of the two not zero, is what a cloned authenticator's does, and WebAuthn calls it a signal rather than a proof: two copies of the key in use, an authenticator that malfunctions and two assertions verified out of order look the same. So the API refuses that sign-in, stores nothing from it, records signin.fail with the reason, and tells the user in GET /api/v1/me. It does not lock the passkey: a lock would let a faulty authenticator shut its owner out, and the owner, once told, is the one who knows whether the other copy is theirs and removes the passkey if it is not.

Decision

No WebAuthn library and no attestation. The code that decides who someone is should be read whole by whoever reviews it, and the part a library would bring, a CBOR decoder, is small enough to write and to fuzz. Attestation would certify the authenticator's make, but the synced passkeys most people hold carry none, so asking for it would refuse them or prove nothing. device_bound_only reads the Backup Eligibility flag in the authenticator data, which needs no attestation; it is the authenticator's own statement, which an installation that must prove its hardware cannot rest on.

Permissions

PermissionAllows
workflow:readSee the YAML, the resolved graph, the version history and the schedule.
workflow:runStart a manual run, cancel it, replay it, approve or reject a waiting run.
workflow:writeRegister a new version, change triggers, rename, move between namespaces the principal owns on both sides.
workflow:deleteDelete the workflow and its versions. Only owner holds it.
run:readSee run state, per-step state, timings and log lines.
run:read_dataSee a run's inputs and envelope contents and download artifacts, not only state and digests.
secret:usePush a version that names a namespace secret, for its steps to mount. Checked at the push, against the principal pushing; running the workflow afterwards takes workflow:run alone. Never allows reading a value.
secret:writeDeclare, change and delete the namespace's secrets, and write a builtin value. Never allows reading one. Reading the declarations takes workflow:read. Both count at namespace scope only, since a declaration serves every workflow of the namespace.
grant:manageGrant and revoke access at this scope.
Decision

secret:use is checked when a version is pushed, against whoever pushes it, and never when the workflow runs. Writing a secret's name into a workflow is what sends its value into a container, so the check sits with whoever put the reference there. An operator then runs a workflow that uses secrets without holding them, which is how a colleague launches a job without being trusted with its credentials. A version naming a secret, pushed by a principal without secret:use in the namespace, is refused with 403. A version accepted stays runnable after its pusher loses the permission, since what was checked is the naming, which is done; the value behind a name is withdrawn at its declaration, under secret:write.

Roles

Rolereadrunwritedatasecretdeletegrant
vieweryesnononononono
operatornoyesnonononono
editoryesyesyesyesyesnono
owneryesyesyesyesyesyesyes
ColumnPermissions
readworkflow:read, run:read
runworkflow:run, run:read
writeworkflow:write, secret:use
datarun:read_data
secretsecret:write
deleteworkflow:delete
grantgrant:manage

viewer, operator and editor are the read, run and edit roles; owner exists because someone has to be able to share. A role holds every permission of each column it says yes to, so each of the nine sits in one column, run:read in two.

  • operator deliberately lacks workflow:read, so a colleague can launch a job without seeing the queries, endpoints and business rules inside it. It holds run:read, so it follows the runs of what it may run, the ones it starts among them: their state and log lines, and never run:read_data, so their payloads stay out of its reach. Someone who needs both holds both roles.
  • secret:use sits with workflow:write because it is checked at the push, which is writing: editor and owner hold it.
  • workflow:delete is the owner's alone. Every change an editor makes is a new version the history keeps; a deletion takes the versions with it, and nothing brings them back.
  • The secret column is secret:write: editor holds it by default, and a deny takes it away where only owners should say where a value lives.

Scopes and resolution

  • A grant binds one principal, one scope and either one role or a deny. The scope is written NS for a namespace or NS/workflow for a single workflow: finance, finance/monthly-invoicing. An optional expiry ends it without anyone remembering to revoke it.
  • Effective permissions are the union of every applying grant: the principal's own and its groups', at both scopes.
  • A workflow-scope grant only adds. Only an explicit deny removes, and it wins over any allow at any scope. A deny names one permission, never a role, since the payloads kept out of reach are run:read_data alone and no role is that.
  • secret:use and secret:write come from namespace grants alone, since a declaration serves every workflow of the namespace: an editor or owner of one workflow holds neither, there or anywhere. A deny of either on one workflow still takes it away there.
  • A grant or a deny ends at the instant its expiry names: one ending at midnight holds until the last instant before it, and not at midnight. A deny that ends stops denying the same way.
  • Removing a workflow removes the grants on it, and removing a namespace every grant in it, so that a workflow created again under the same name starts with none of the old one's. Who granted what, and when, stays in the audit log.
  • No matching grant means refusal: the same 404 whether the workflow is absent or merely invisible, so listing cannot discover names.
  • Every user owns a personal namespace named after their login, which they cannot delete or rename, and which is removed with its user where it holds nothing. Their first sign-in creates it, with a passkey or a password, an enrolment that signs them in included, with its built-in identity and a grant of owner to them, so that they can act in it and share it; the audit log records installation as having done so, since nobody asked for it.

The API's first path segment decides the route, so these words cannot name a namespace or a login, and are refused at creation from v0.3.0:

Reserved
auth, me, users, groups, service-accounts, namespaces, runners, runner-pools, bus, tasks, bricks, runs, artifacts
Decision

Grants live in the platform database and are managed through the API and its clients, never in the workflow YAML. In the file, workflow:write would equal grant:manage: an editor could make themselves owner in the same commit. It also keeps the file portable between installations.

Administrators

  • A platform administrator manages users, groups, namespaces, quotas, runners, runner policies and the authentication policy.
  • Administering is asked as grant:manage at the installation, which the routes marked administrator only require. An administrator holds it there and nothing else, and only through a token with no scope (Sessions and tokens); in a namespace, an administrator holds what their grants give, as anybody does.
  • An administrator holds no implicit run:read_data. Reading another namespace's payloads means granting themselves access first, which is audited and notifies the namespace's owner: a notification in the owner's GET /api/v1/me, because an owner does not read the audit log, and the people whose data it is should hear of it from the installation itself.
  • An administrator may create a grant in any namespace, for anybody, as a power of the installation rather than through grant:manage there, since namespaces and their owners are theirs to manage; the namespace's owner is told of each, as of a grant an administrator gives themselves. Listing and revoking grants are grant:manage's alone: an administrator reads and revokes through a grant, as anybody does.
  • An administrator's own access is theirs, that of a group they are in, and that of a service account of a namespace they own, whose tokens they may mint. A role given to any of these, or a deny taken from one, is told to the namespace's owners however the administrator came to share, since an owner who also administers the installation widens their own access all the same, and the other owners are the ones to hear of it. The administrator who acted is not told what they have just done.
  • So is an administrator's own group membership: putting themselves in a group tells the owners of each namespace where its grants give a role, and taking themselves out of one, or removing a group they are in, the owners of each namespace where its denies took a permission away, admin_access_widened with the group's grant, since joining a group is the other way to grant oneself what the group holds.
  • A notification owed to a group is written once for each of its members, so that one member dismissing it dismisses it for nobody else; a service account holding the owner role is told as itself, since its token reads GET /api/v1/me as a user's does. It is written in the transaction that writes the grant, so that no administrator's grant is made untold.
  • The owner told is the principal the namespace's record names. A namespace from before v0.3.0 names none: it becomes shared, since an administrator made it for whoever used it and v0.2 had nobody to name, and every principal holding the owner role on it is told instead.
  • Where a route speaks of a namespace the caller owns, as for service accounts and their tokens, it means one on which the caller holds an unexpired grant of the owner role, its own or one of its groups', on the namespace rather than on one of its workflows. A deny beside it leaves the namespace owned, since a deny takes one permission away wherever it is asked and never a role. An administrator owns what such a grant gives and nothing more; the bootstrap token owns every namespace until it ends.
  • Where a route speaks of a principal holding a grant in a namespace, as for who reads the namespace's record, it means an unexpired grant carrying a role, its own or one of its groups', on the namespace or on one of its workflows. A deny alone is not one: it gives nothing, and a namespace where a principal holds only denies is one it can do nothing in.
  • A notification is kept 90 days from when it was written, or until its reader dismisses it with DELETE /api/v1/me/notifications/{id}: long enough to reach someone back from leave, and bounded so that GET /api/v1/me does not grow for ever. One past its days is removed when its reader next reads GET /api/v1/me, rather than by a sweep of its own, and is never answered either way.
  • Once the bootstrap token has ended, the last administrator who can sign in, not suspended and holding a credential the policy that applies to them signs them in with, is not removed: from then on only an administrator makes another, and an installation nobody can administer is the lockout the bootstrap token lasts until an administrator can sign in to avoid. Until it ends, the token can make another.
  • The first administrator is created with the bootstrap token, by agk user create LOGIN --admin, and the token ends once an administrator it created can sign in to a full session (First run).
  • An administrator who lost what signs them in is issued a recovery code by another administrator, never by themselves; where none can sign in, agentiik-api recover on the installation's host issues one, and every administrator is told in GET /api/v1/me (Authentication).

What sharing does not expose

  • Secret values, at any role. workflow:read at namespace scope shows the declarations (names, providers, paths and mount points), and a grant on one workflow shows none; the value only ever exists inside a container.
  • Artifacts from another namespace. A presigned URL covers one artifact of one run and expires in minutes.
  • Runner internals. A user never learns which host executed a task beyond its runner name and labels.
  • The existence of workflows they cannot read, in any listing, search result or error message.

Quotas per namespace

QuotaPurpose
max_concurrent_tasksFleet share one namespace can hold at once, so that a fan-out of ten thousand items cannot starve everyone else.
max_runs_per_hourRate limit across every trigger kind, webhooks included: the runs created in the last 60 minutes, a sliding count, taken where every run is created, so that a trigger added later is limited with no counter of its own. Past it the API answers 429 with Retry-After, the whole seconds until one more fits; a scheduled or event firing starts no run and is recorded as a skipped firing, with that reason; and a workflow: step whose call it refuses fails, with that reason. The runs are counted under a lock on the namespace, so that two replicas of the API creating runs at once count one after the other rather than both creating the one run that fits; a namespace without the quota takes no lock. Sliding rather than per clock hour, which would let twice the quota through across the turn of an hour.
max_artifact_bytesTotal live artifact storage: the bytes of the namespace's live artifacts, each digest once, since identical bytes are one object in a namespace, and of the writes not yet referenced. A write is counted from before its bytes are read, since a runner posts an object before the controller hears of the result naming it, and room is made under a lock on the namespace, so that two writes that each fit alone cannot both pass; a namespace without the quota takes no lock. A write past it is refused by the built-in store with 507, and its step fails on the platform's account; an object the namespace already holds as a live artifact takes no room. An artifact's room is free again at its expiry, not at the purge that retires it. Envelopes are posted the same way and are held to it while their upload lasts; a push is not counted.
max_retention_daysUpper bound on what the namespace may ask to keep: an output's retain, and defaults.retain, which dates a run's envelopes and logs. A workflow declaring neither is kept that long, so that nothing is kept for ever.
max_run_durationUpper bound on a workflow's root timeout, and the bound of a run whose workflow writes none, so no run holds capacity longer than the operator accepts: a run asking more is held to it rather than refused, read at every pass (Deadlines).
allowed_runner_poolsRunner pools, by name, whose runners this namespace's steps may be sent to, each one a pool that exists when the list is written. A step's runs_on chooses among the pools both sides allow: those the list names that accept the namespace, or every pool that accepts it where the namespace sets no list. A step whose labels select only a pool outside the list fails at dispatch with exit code 125, naming the pool and the list; a redemption by a runner of such a pool, for a task that waited while the list changed, is refused with 422. A push is not checked against the list, since the list and the pools can both change before a run of the version is dispatched.

From v0.3.0, the six sit together under quotas on the namespace's record, allowed_runner_pools among them. Every quota is optional when written. max_concurrent_tasks and max_retention_days always hold a value, 20 and 90 until an administrator sets another, and a write that leaves either out keeps the value it has. The other four bound nothing until they are set, and a write that leaves one out removes its bound. The two were a namespace's bounds in v0.2 and the four are new, so an upgrade refuses nothing a namespace was allowed. The four counts are whole numbers from 1, max_run_duration is written as a step's timeout, and allowed_runner_pools names at least one pool: an empty list is refused, because a pool's own empty list of namespaces means every one, and the same spelling here would be read as its opposite.

Sessions and tokens

ClientCredentialRules
web consoleopaque session identifier, 256 bits, in the cookie __Host-agentiik_session: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, no Domain and no expiry of its ownOpened by a sign-in on the sign-in page, kept as its SHA-256, revocable server-side. Ends 12 hours after its last request, 30 days after it opened however it is used, at a sign-out, and with its user or the credential that opened it; opens nothing while its user is suspended. Records the credential that opened it, so that what it may do is read at every request from that credential and the policy that applies then, not by convention: one a password opened where the policy requires a passkey enrols passkeys and sets its password, and nothing else (Authentication).
API, agk, mobilebearer tokenHeld by a user or a service account, never a group, which holds no credential of its own. Stored hashed, shown once, revocable one by one, listed with last use and device label. Expires after 90 days unless asked otherwise, and after a year at most. At most 100 live ones per principal.
webhookHMAC over the raw body with a per-trigger secret, a bearer token bound to a service account, or a client certificateAuthenticates the caller, not a user.
A request carrying a sessionIs answered
GET, HEAD or OPTIONSAs the session's user, from whatever page, since SameSite=Lax lets a link followed from another site carry the cookie, and what it reads is not that site's to see: the API answers no cross-origin read.
any other methodOnly where its one Origin header is the public URL's origin, and 403 otherwise, before the session is looked up, so that a page of another host of the same site, which SameSite=Lax counts as the same site, neither acts on the session nor keeps it open.
with a bearer token, or a second session cookie400: a request is answered as one principal, and which of two was meant is not the API's to guess.
a session that opens nothing401 with one sentence, whatever the reason: never opened here, signed out, revoked, idle, 30 days old, its user suspended or removed, the credential that opened it removed, or, read from the policy at that request, a password's where passwords are now forbidden or a synced passkey's where device_bound_only now applies.
a session that may only enrol403, "this session enrols passkeys and nothing else", on every route but the passkey registration, the setting of the password that opened it, and the sign-out, which read the session themselves.
Decision

Twelve hours idle, thirty days at most, and no expiry on the cookie. A working day with its breaks is one sign-in, and a browser left overnight on a shared machine is signed out by the morning. A tab left open on a dashboard never goes idle, so without a limit its session would be a credential for good, which no token is allowed to be; thirty days has its holder prove who they are once a month, with the passkey and the policy of that day. With no expiry of its own, the cookie goes when the browser forgets it, and the server ends it either way.

An API token's expiry is 90 days by default, so a token forgotten in a script stops on its own within a season, and a year at most, so that no token is a credential for good and every one is renewed by someone who still means it. An expiry up to a minute past the year is taken as asked, since a client computing a year from now on a clock a little ahead of the installation's would otherwise be refused the year it may have. A principal holds at most 100 live tokens, neither revoked nor expired, counted under a lock on the principal so that two mints at once cannot both take the last place: enough for every machine and script one is used from, and few enough that a script minting one at every run and never revoking it is stopped while its principal's listing can still be read.

A service account's tokens follow the same rules, and are minted, listed and revoked by whoever owns its namespace (Administrators). A service account's own token mints none for that account, 403, since a token that minted its successor would be a credential for good. The rule is per account: a service account holding the owner role owns its namespace as any principal does, and mints for the other service accounts of it, so two such accounts may renew each other, which is an owner's decision and visible in the grant list. No token is minted for a namespace's built-in identity, NS/agentiik, 422: it is the installation's unattended identity, which the runs nobody started are attributed to, and a token of it would let whoever holds it act as those runs, with the grants an owner gave them for that alone, for up to a year past that person's own access. A script is given a service account of its own.

A token's value is agktoken_ and 43 base64url characters, 256 bits from a cryptographic source. The prefix says what it is to whoever finds one in a log or a bug report, so that it can be recognised and revoked.

A token narrowed by a scope mints no token, since the one it minted would carry its principal's rights and not its narrowing, and it lists and revokes itself alone, since managing credentials is none of the nine. The bootstrap token mints none either, answering 403 with a sentence that names agk user create LOGIN --admin: its one lasting use is to create the first administrator, and a token it minted would outlive it.

A token's optional scope is {permissions, within}, at least one of the two present: permissions the permissions it keeps, within the namespaces and workflows it reaches, written as a grant's scope is. On every request its rights are the principal's intersected with both, so a scope can only narrow, and naming a permission the principal lacks grants nothing.

An administrator's powers pass through a token only where its scope does not narrow them away. A token with no scope carries them. A within takes them away, since it names namespaces and workflows and administering is the installation's. A permissions list keeps only the permissions it names, and administering is none of the nine. So a token an administrator mints to run one workflow never creates a user.

A namespace in within reaches every workflow of it, as a grant on the namespace does. A workflow reaches that workflow and not its namespace, so a route asked about the namespace, such as its secrets' declarations or its grants, answers the token as it answers a caller holding nothing there. The namespace's record is still read through it, since reading it is none of the nine and the workflow cannot be reached without it.

A bearer token that opens nothing is answered 401 with one sentence, whatever the reason: no token this installation issued, one revoked or expired, or one whose holder is suspended. Saying which would tell somebody guessing tokens whether they had a real one. Once the bootstrap token has ended, the sentence adds that it ended then, since the line left in .env is the likeliest token to stop working, and its hash is forgotten, so the API cannot tell whether it was the one presented.

a token that only starts one workflow, from v0.3.0
{ "scope": { "permissions": ["workflow:run"], "within": ["finance/monthly-invoicing"] } }

Authorisation is asked again when a run is let in, because a trigger armed months ago can fire long after the grant that armed it, and a run waiting on its concurrency group is let in long after the request that created it was answered. From v0.3.0 the controller asks, of every run whatever created it, whether the principal it is attributed to still holds workflow:run on its workflow: before the run's concurrency group is asked about it, and on every pass until it is let in, never after. Before the group, because a run with cancel_in_progress takes its group by cancelling the run holding it, and one nobody may start would otherwise end somebody else's before being refused itself. The question is package access's over the grants the database holds, as the API's is, since two answers to one question drift unless they are one function. A run whose principal may no longer start it ends cancelled before any task, with a reason naming what lapsed:

a run refused at creation, from v0.3.0
cancelled: finance/agentiik no longer holds workflow:run on finance/monthly-invoicing: grant 01JQ3M8T (operator on the namespace finance) expired at 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z

The reason is on the run, where GET /api/v1/runs/{id}, agk status and agk run show it. cancelled rather than failed, because nothing in the workflow failed; and a run rather than a silence, so that whoever armed the trigger sees why it did nothing. It starts P no longer holds workflow:run on S, and goes on:

Where the principal standsThe reason goes on
a grant that gave it expiredgrant 01JQ3M8T (operator on the namespace finance) expired at 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z
a grant that gave it was revokedgrant 01JQ3M8T (operator on the workflow finance/monthly-invoicing) was revoked at 2026-10-01T09:12:00Z
a deny of workflow:run appliesa deny applies
a user suspended or removed, a service account removedit holds nothing there
operator, once the bootstrap token has endedthe bootstrap token ended at T, when the first administrator enrolled a passkey
no grant gives it, or none ended since the run was asked forIn place of the whole: P does not hold workflow:run on S: no grant gives it there, and for NS/agentiik, , and a namespace's built-in identity holds none until an owner gives it one.
  • Where several grants gave it, the one that ended last is named, since its end is the one the run is refused for. A run somebody asked for was authorised when they asked, so only a grant that ended after it was created is named; a run a trigger created may name one that ended long before.
  • A run already let in goes on: the question is asked of a run not yet let in, and a run the bootstrap token started that is still waiting when the token ends is cancelled naming the end.
  • The whole account goes to the audit log, as run.cancel by installation in the run's namespace, with the principal, the workflow, the reason and account: the group a grant was written for, the deny and whom it names, the suspension or the removal, and who revoked the grant.
Decision

The reason names less than the audit log records. Whoever holds run:read on the workflow reads the run, a viewer among them, and which groups somebody is in, which denies are written and whether an account is suspended or gone are the business of those who manage them. So the reason names a grant by its identifier, role and scope, says a deny applies without saying whose, and says the principal holds nothing there without saying why; the account behind it is in the audit log, for those who read it.

§

Runtime architecture

The controller holds the state and makes every decision; runners execute and decide nothing. No runner reaches the database or the secret store: it receives tasks over the bus and gets short-lived tokens and presigned URLs for everything else. A compromised runner therefore exposes the tasks it runs, not the installation, though on MinIO or S3 it can also overwrite objects of those tasks' namespaces (see What this does not defend against).

From trigger to result

  1. A trigger fires. The API authenticates it, authorises it, resolves the ref to a commit, writes the run and notifies the controller.
  2. The controller evaluates the graph at that commit and finds the steps whose every declared input port is already satisfied.
  3. For each of them it creates one task per shard and publishes those tasks on the queue of the one pool whose labels include every label of the step's runs_on, or of the pool default where it names none. It does not choose a machine, and it does not start one.
  4. A registered runner, already polling, takes a task from that queue when it has room; nothing is pushed to it. It fetches what the task names, runs one container and destroys it (see Runner).
  5. It publishes a result on the bus. The controller consumes it, writes the new state, evaluates the graph again and publishes whatever has just become runnable.
  6. Steps 3 to 5 repeat until nothing is runnable, and the run reaches a terminal state.
Decision

The runner is not the ephemeral thing; the container is. A runner is a long-lived agent that pulls work; the platform cannot start one, reach one or place work on a named one. That makes a runner in a demilitarised zone, on bare metal or in someone else's network a firewall rule rather than a project, and, since a runner holds no graph, losing one costs only the tasks in its hands. Capacity grows by starting more agents, never by the platform reaching out.

Controller

  • Evaluates the graph on every task state change and publishes the tasks that have become ready.
  • Holds concurrency-group locks, per-step parallelism counters and per-namespace quotas.
  • Asks again, of every run not yet let in, whether the principal it is attributed to still holds workflow:run on its workflow: before its concurrency group, on every pass until it is let in, and never after. From v0.3.0 a run that fails it ends cancelled before any task, with a reason naming what lapsed, recorded as run.cancel by installation (Sessions and tokens).
  • Emits the notification events that the API turns into push messages: failure, approval requested, completion of a run the recipient started.
  • From v0.3.0, runs the retention purges, the collection and the orphan sweep while it leads, and no other instance does (What each purge acts on).
  • Runs as several instances with one active at a time, elected by a session-level PostgreSQL advisory lock. Failover is a state resume, never a rebuild: the state lives in the database, not in the process. See How the API and the controller stay in step.
  • Stops, rather than retrying in place, once it can no longer reach the database, the bus or its lock, or once the control plane's bus credential expires; its supervisor starts it again as a standby. Its connections set TCP keepalives, so a controller cut off without a reset loses its session, and the lock with it, within half a minute rather than the operating system's two hours.
Decision

A controller that loses what it stands on ends rather than retrying: one that retried in place would be the partitioned former holder the fence exists to refuse.

Task bus

NATS JetStream with WorkQueue retention: a message leaves the stream once it is acknowledged. The control plane creates one durable pull consumer per runner pool, when the pool is created and again for every pool as the API starts, default included, never when a runner asks for its bus credential; a bus that refuses one refuses the API's start, and every runner of the pool takes from it and creates none. A runner asks for a batch only when it has room, so distribution follows each host's real capacity without the controller modelling load.

Delivery is at least once, so a task can arrive twice. Its idempotency key, run_id/step/attempt/shard, the redemption that binds it to one runner, and a record each host keeps of the keys it took make that harmless. A runner handles each message in the order Runner sets out: it writes the key down, redeems the grant, and only then acknowledges the message, before it pulls or starts anything.

The record is one file per key, <work root>/.keys/<run>/<step>/<attempt>[/<index>-<of>].json under AGK_RUNNER_WORKDIR, outside every task directory since those go with their containers. It is pruned 7 days after its last write, the longest a message waits on the stream.

The record keepsNever
the key, the state, the exit code (a stopped container's 137 or 143, and 121 for refused outputs, included), when it started and ended; where the daemon cannot give the span after the exit, the span from the dispatch to the moment the exit was readthe message or its grant
what the ending left, by reference: each port's envelope digest and item count, each artifact's digest and size, the log's URI and line counta payload: the envelopes are in the store before the ending is written
What goes wrongWhat follows
the host dies before redeeming, step 2It acknowledged nothing, so the pool consumer's AckWait, one minute, passes and the bus hands the message to another runner of the pool.
the host dies after redeemingIts heartbeat stops, the task becomes lost and comes back only as Back to pending says. The message, if never acknowledged, comes round and is refused with 409.
the acknowledgement of step 3 never reaches the busThe message comes round after AckWait. Every other runner is refused it at the redemption; the holder finds the key in flight or ended on its host. Nothing runs twice.
the redemption of step 2 is refused, or gets no answerThe runner acknowledges the message only once an answer says whose the task is, or once it has reported that no container ran: The task message says which answer leads where.
the requeue of a lost task reaches the host that already ended its keyNothing is redeemed. The host reports the ending it recorded under the requeue's task_id, then acknowledges. The controller takes that ending from a runner that redeemed an earlier dispatch of the key, and the brick does not run twice.
the requeue reaches the host still running its keyNothing is redeemed and nothing acknowledged there, and the message comes round after AckWait to whichever runner of the pool takes it. Another runner redeems and runs it, which is what a requeue is for, so two containers of the key can run at once; only an idempotent step is requeued. Back on this host it is refused again until the key has ended, then answered from the record. A host only cut off costs its key one requeue, not two.
the result could not be publishedIt is kept under <work root>/.results, its key stays in the heartbeat, and it goes out once the bus answers or the agent is back. A copy within two minutes is dropped by the stream, and a later one is no news.
the agent stopped between the recorded ending and the publicationBefore it runs a task, the runner writes down the task_id it owes a result to, as <work root>/.results/<task_id>.owed, since the record keeps the key and not the dispatch. The entry goes once the result is kept or the bus has it. The agent that comes back reads the key's ending from the record, keeps the result under that task_id, names the key from its first heartbeat and publishes it. A dispatch whose key never ended is owed nothing, and the record names its key as taken. Nothing is declared lost and nothing runs twice.
a task waits on a full pool's queue, or behind a slow pullIt is never lost for the wait, but the wait counts against its deadline (Task states).
its deadline passes before anyone redeems itEvery redemption answers 401, the grant having expired with the deadline. The runner holding the message reports the task timed_out with no container ran, which ends the dispatch and binds that runner, then acknowledges, and the step's retry reads it as a timeout. A message no runner ever takes ends only with the run's own timeout, and a run without one waits.
Decision

A runner redeems before it acknowledges, and acknowledges before it pulls. The redemption decides who runs a task, and the bus lets go of a message only once the database says whose it is. So a host that dies before redeeming leaves its message to the bus, one that dies after leaves a bound task to the heartbeat, and nothing sweeps a task nobody redeemed. Acknowledging at the end would make AckWait as long as the longest step.

The cost, accepted: secret values are read at the redemption, before the pull, rather than just before the container starts.

Decision

A host answers a requeue of a key it already ended with that ending, rather than dropping it. Nobody would redeem the requeue, so the run would wait on it until its timeout. Taking the answer only from a runner that redeemed an earlier dispatch of the key keeps a host's reach to the tasks it was given.

A task carries no payload and no secret value; see The task message.

Runner

StepThe runnerDocker Engine API v1.56
firstSubscribes to agentiik.stops over its own bus connection, before it takes anything, so a task it holds can be stopped from the moment it holds it (Channels). A subscription the bus refuses or does not confirm ends the agent at start, since a runner that cannot hear stops would run every stopped container to its deadline.
1When it has room, pulls from its pool's consumer (the pool's subject is the filter) as many tasks as AGK_RUNNER_CONCURRENCY less those it holds, so a full host asks for nothing; the pull is a 20 s long poll, answered as soon as one task is there. A key this host already ended is answered from the record, and one it still has in flight is left on the queue; neither is redeemed. Of the rest, before anything is written down: a message whose image is not name@sha256 is reported as no container ran, on the platform's account, then acknowledged, since no runner of any pool could ever run it; one whose namespace AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES leaves out, whose runs_on names a label this runner does not claim (a join token may allow fewer labels than its pool carries), or whose declared resources would take the host past its declared capacity with what it already holds, is put back on the queue for another runner or a later pull. Anything put back is held back one second from every runner; one put back for want of room does not pause the runner, since the next message may fit, and any other does, this runner taking nothing more for that second. Only then does it write each remaining key down in its record as dispatched (Task bus), so a message it put back is never found in flight when it comes round.
2Redeems the task's grant for the repository tree at the commit, presigned URLs to the input envelopes and artifacts, the secret values and one upload policy. The redemption binds the task to this runner, and the heartbeat holds it from then on. The task message says what any other answer binds and what the runner does then.
3Acknowledges the message, now that the database says whose the task is.
4Reads the record again and refuses a key that has already ended, before a network, a pull or a secret is written. Then fetches each input envelope through the redemption's URL and holds it to the digest and item count the message gives, lays the tree out in a directory of its own under <work root>/.trees with each file held to its digest, and prepares the mounts. A task whose inputs or tree are not what the message names is refused before any container exists, and before its image is pulled.
5Runs the host's pre_task hooks, if any, from v0.9.0 (Runner-side hooks). Creates one container, pulling the image by digest as part of the create, bounded by the task's deadline: a deadline that passes during the pull or while the manifest is read ends the task timed_out with no container ran, the log saying how long the pull ran, and a stop that landed during the pull ends it cancelled. A signature is verified where policy requires it from v0.8.0 (Supply chain). Starts the container and publishes running, attaches to it, samples its statistics while it runs, waits for it to exit and publishes publishing. Its log is shipped while the container runs (Observability).ContainerCreate (POST /containers/create), ContainerStart (POST /containers/{id}/start), ContainerAttach, ContainerWait, ContainerLogs, ContainerStats (GET /containers/{id}/stats), for the usage block
6Collects the output envelopes, artifacts and exit code, posts the outputs under the upload policy, and closes the log with its closing chunk. Only then writes the key's ending (temporary file, sync, rename), so every envelope the ending names is already in the store.
7Destroys the container, its working directory and every tree laid out for its key, then writes the result under <work root>/.results, once the log is closed, and publishes it on its own results subject, taking it away once the bus has it. A result the bus did not take is published again, after a restart too, and its key stays in the heartbeat until it is out. It writes down the dispatch it owes a result to before step 5, and takes that away once the result is kept.ContainerRemove
throughoutEmits a heartbeat. A prolonged absence moves the task to lost.
throughoutFollows the daemon event stream to catch container exits it did not cause, an out-of-memory kill for instance.GET /events

The runner speaks Docker Engine API v1.56 at most and negotiates down to what the daemon offers, refusing a daemon below v1.41.

A runner's policy is written in three places, each for what only it knows. Restricting a pool or a host to a list of namespaces is how a namespace gets dedicated capacity without a separate installation.

WhereHoldsEnforced by
the pool, set through the APIaccepted namespaces; ceilings on cpu, memory and pidsThe controller, at dispatch: a step whose labels select no pool, or more than one, among the pools that accept the run's namespace and that the namespace's allowed_runner_pools names, where it names any, or whose pool one side refuses, is not published and fails on the infrastructure's account (exit code 125), every shard of the step on the pass that finds it, naming the labels, or the pool and which side refused it. Resources over a ceiling are capped on the task message, and a step that asks for none is given the ceiling. The API checks both sides again at the redemption: 422.
/etc/agentiik/runner.tomlthe host's own settings: the require_userns_remap floor, the stop grace, security profiles, allowed capabilities, ulimits, host caps and helper, the /agk/bin/agk of a script step: the installed helper by default; a named path is used as written, and in the container form must be at the same path in the agent's container and on the hostThe runner.
AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACESa narrower list for one host, sent at joinThe runner, which puts the message back on the queue before redeeming, and the API, which answers 403, so another runner of the pool takes the task.

A task above the host's declared capacity is put back on the queue (Sizing); one above a pool's ceiling is capped. There is no disk ceiling, because nothing can enforce one.

The agent is agk-runner, one program shipped as a container and as a single static binary run as a system service (see Installing a runner), holding three capabilities and no other privilege. It opens no inbound port in either form: every connection is outbound, to the API, the bus, the object store and the registry.

§

Component communication

One rule shapes every channel: the less trusted side always initiates. A runner opens no listening port and is never connected to (see the runner decision).

Channels

Decision

No plaintext path means nothing crosses a network without TLS, and every connection the programs open holds TLS 1.2 as its floor. A runner refuses a bus address, a presigned URL or an upload policy that would cross a network in plaintext, and refuses a daemon anywhere but on its local socket, even when the API handed it that address: the check sits at each end rather than trusting the other. The one hop allowed without TLS, from a terminator to a program serving none itself, is named in Cryptography in use.

Stops

A stop is $defs/stop in wire.schema.json, closed: task, the idempotency key, which is what the runner records and its heartbeat names, and reason. Only the control plane publishes one; every runner subscribes over its own connection before it takes anything, and the runner holding the key sends its container SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after stop_grace. A stop nobody can read is reported and not acted on, and the heartbeat's cancel is the backstop (Heartbeat).

A runner stops a key once, whichever channel names it first: the bus and the heartbeat's cancel both repeat a stop while the container winds down, and the driver is asked again only where it could not reach the daemon. The first stop decides what the runner reports: timed_out for a deadline heard on the bus, cancelled otherwise. A heartbeat's cancel carries no reason, so a key it reaches first is reported cancelled, and the ending the controller recorded stands either way. A stop for a key the runner does not hold, counting those an earlier agent on the host took and never ended, is passed over without asking the daemon. A stop the daemon refuses for a running container is sent again, from 1 s doubling to 10 s, until the daemon takes it or the task ends. A stop for a container an earlier agent left running is carried through to SIGKILL however soon the caller gives up.

on agentiik.stops
{ "task": "01JMZ8V1P9C4XQ7K2N4D6F8H0A/invoice/2/3/8", "reason": "sibling_failed" }
reasonWhenThe task ends
supersededA merge: first lifted on another edge, and nobody needs what this task would publish. It also names the tasks of that step not yet started, which never start.cancelled
sibling_failedfail_fast: another shard of the step failed. It also names the shards not yet started, which never start.cancelled
deadlineThe run's root timeout passed.timed_out
cancelledA principal holding workflow:run, or a concurrency group, cancelled the run.cancelled

A stop for a task nobody holds is sent all the same, since a task may have been published before its dispatch was recorded.

A superseded or sibling_failed task ends cancelled when its stop goes out, not when its container exits, and its step is judged then. The evaluator decides it, so agk run --local and a server give the same state for the same history. The runner's later report adds the exit code, the log and the usage and nothing else: a container that exited 0 in the moment before the stop reached it still reads cancelled and publishes nothing. It holds no slot of max_concurrent_tasks from that pass.

Decision

Waiting on the report would hold a fail_fast step on containers being called off, and on a server would wait on a bus that may lose the stop; the heartbeat's cancel repeats a stop only for a row that already reads cancelled.

Decision

A stop names the key and no runner, and every runner hears it: the evaluator that decides it knows nothing of runners, and a dispatch taken and not yet redeemed is bound to none, so a subject every runner hears is the one place its holder is sure to be listening.

What has to be open

HostInboundOutbound
API and controller443, from clients and runnersdatabase, bus, secret store, push services
runnernothing443 to the API, the bus port, the object store, the registry
database, secret storetheir own port, from the control plane onlynothing

How the API and the controller stay in step

  • They share the database and nothing else. There is no remote call between them, in either direction.
  • When the API creates a run it commits the row and issues a NOTIFY carrying the run identifier. PostgreSQL delivers such an event only once the transaction commits, and only to sessions currently listening.
  • A controller that was restarting therefore misses notifications, so it also sweeps for actionable work on a fixed interval, which a notification does not reset. The notification is a latency optimisation; the sweep is the correctness guarantee.
  • The sweep looks at four kinds of run: one never decided, one whose clock has come round (a retry's backoff or the root timeout), one holding a task whose message never went, and one somebody has asked to cancel. A run waiting on tasks in flight is none of these. What it waits for makes it due at the moment it arrives: a result, and a loss, whether the heartbeat declared it or a runner reported it. A pass that then finds nothing new takes no decision: the sequence stays where it was, nothing is written but the clock it found, and the run drops out of the sweep again.
  • A second channel, agentiik_task_log, serves log streams: a log shipment notifies it with the task's idempotency key, and every API node listens on one connection and sweeps its open streams every 5 s, so a missed notification delays a line and loses none.
  • A notification carries only an identifier, far below the documented 8000-byte payload limit.
Decision

A pass that changes nothing is not a decision. The sequence is what tells a stale copy of a run from a current one; counting every pass would rewrite the same document at a new number every ten seconds for every waiting run, and read that moved number as something to act on. A clock put back is written only over the row as the pass read it, so a loss landing while a pass decides nothing is still heard.

Decision

The active controller holds a session-level advisory lock, not a lease with an expiry. PostgreSQL documents that such a lock "is held until explicitly released or the session ends", so nothing has to invent a timeout or trust a clock: the lock frees itself when the process exits or the server notices the connection is gone. Standbys retry the non-blocking variant and take over the instant it succeeds. Because a partitioned former holder may not yet know it has lost, every controller write carries the lock's acquisition counter as a fencing token and a write bearing an older counter is refused. Election alone would not be safe; the fencing token is what makes it so.

The task message

A task message names everything the runner needs and contains nothing sensitive. It carries no business payload, no secret value and no URL that would work without the grant, a short-lived token scoped to that run alone.

published by the controller, consumed by one runner

}

A runner redeems before it acknowledges the message and pulls the image (Runner). The first redemption with an answer to give binds the task to that runner, and one refused binds nothing. A drain ordered between the take and the redemption puts the message back at once, redeeming nothing, unless an earlier agent on this host held its key.

A redemption answersIt bindsThe runner then
200the task, to this runnerAcknowledges the message, pulls the image and runs the task.
403: this runner is draining or revoked and does not hold the task, or its AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES leaves out the run's namespacenothingClears the key from its record and puts the message back on the queue, held back a second from every runner, for another runner of the pool.
409: another runner's task, or one that is overnothingAcknowledges the message and starts nothing.
422: nothing to answer with, ever: no commit, version or tree recorded for the task, a secret the namespace does not declare or holds no value for, a pool that does not accept the run's namespace, or a pool the namespace's allowed_runner_pools leaves out; or a 200 from the API (it echoes the task_id) whose document this runner cannot read or that does not answer the message: another input digest, a secret the message does not name, a tree path leaving /agk/repo, an upload policy for another namespacenothingReports that no container ran, then acknowledges. One that dies in between leaves the message to the next runner of the pool.
no answer at all, a 401, any other 5xx, any status this table does not name, or a 200 that does not echo the task_id asked for (a proxy's page): the grant expired or opens nothing, the runner's own credential was refused, or a failure that may pass, such as an input or a secret its store could not read this timeperhaps: the answer may be lost after the bindingKeeps the key, names it in its heartbeat and redeems again, from 1 s apart doubling to 30 s, acknowledging nothing. Once the deadline the message carries has passed, no answer can come, since the grant expires with it: it reports the task timed_out with no container ran, then acknowledges.

A runner that already holds the task is not asked its standing, its pool or its namespaces again, since those decide who takes a task: it redeems again once drained or revoked, since finishing what it holds is what a drain and a grace leave it to do. For a task nobody holds they are checked in that order: a draining or revoked runner gets 403 before its pool is asked, since a 422 would have it report the task and so bind it, and a pool that does not accept the namespace, or that the namespace does not allow, gets 422 before a narrowing that leaves it out, since putting the message back would only hand it round the pool. The controller publishes no task to a pool the namespace does not allow, so a redemption refused for that is a task that waited while an administrator changed the namespace's list.

A fetch that fails after a 200 is tried again with the same redemption, whose URLs hold until the deadline, and the secrets are not read a second time. A fetch still failing when the deadline passes is reported timed_out with no container ran. Bytes that are not what the message names, or a message no runner can run (one that contradicts its key, or names a workflow, deadline, timeout or network nothing reads), are reported failed with no container ran, on the platform's account.

The holder asking again, after a lost answer or after a restart, is given the same task with fresh URLs and the secret values read from the store again, since nothing keeps them. A value rotated in between arrives rotated, and a runner adopting a running container then masks a value the container does not hold (Secrets).

A value that is not UTF-8 travels as "encoding": "base64". The fields are the store's own words, the built-in store's above, and a runner posts them as given: a multipart/form-data body of the fields, then key, the prefix and the file's SHA-256, then file, last.

The policy is bound toSo
<namespace>/sha256/Every key is key_prefix and 64 lowercase hex characters: finance/sha256/c1f4a9…d02b. Nothing is written outside the task's namespace.
the runSigned in, as into every presigned URL. It narrows no key: a namespace's objects are shared by all its runs, which is how identical bytes are stored once.
the grant's expiryIt stops working when the task's grant does.
CheckBuilt-in storeMinIO or S3, not built yet
the prefix and the expiryyes: 403to be set as conditions of the policy
a size up to artifact_max_bytesyes: 413to be set as content-length-range
a key of the prefix and 64 lowercase hex characters, and nothing elseyes: 403no: a policy can say only starts-with
bytes that hash to their keyyes, as they arrive, as for a presigned PUT: 400no: the store does not hash
room within the namespace's max_artifact_bytesyes: 507, before the bytes are read where the request states its length, and as soon as they outgrow their room where it does notnot decided: the presigner's quota waits for v0.9.0

The built-in store is the API itself, at /objects/ on a base URL the installation configures, never the request's Host: it answers 201 for an object stored and a refusal with no body, reads at most 64 KiB of form before the file and answers 400 to a form carrying more, and serves an installation that attaches no object store, which no deployment profile does. It is also the only store built so far: the MinIO or S3 column is what their presigner, a v0.9.0 task, has to set.

The redemption hands out a policy whatever room the namespace has left, since a task may write nothing, or only objects the namespace already holds, which take none. The write past the quota is what is refused, and a runner told 507 fails the task with no exit code, on the platform's account, as for any write the store refuses: the brick did what it was asked.

Decision

One policy per task, handed out at the redemption, rather than a URL per object: an output's key is the digest of bytes that do not exist until the container exits, and a policy in the one answer means a task never needs to redeem a second time, reading its secrets again, to learn where its outputs go.

Open question

On MinIO or S3, a runner holding any task of finance can overwrite any object of finance, one other runs already read included. An object is read back against its digest, so this costs availability rather than integrity; what refuses the write itself is not decided.

published by the runner, consumed by the controller

The result is $defs/taskResult in wire.schema.json: outputs by digest, never envelopes, which the controller reads back from the store. Each runner publishes on agentiik.results.<runner>, a subject its bus credential alone may publish on. The controller matches a result on idempotency_key and task_id together, then holds it to the runner that dispatch was bound to:

A resultIs
from the runner the task_id was bound to at redemptiontaken
from another runner, or naming a runner other than its subject'srefused and reported, never applied
saying no container ran, since its grant would not redeem or since its image is not name@sha256, for a dispatch nobody redeemedtaken, and binds the runner that sent it
saying a container ran, for a dispatch nobody redeemed, from a runner that redeemed an earlier dispatch of the keytaken, and binds that runner: a host answering a requeue from its record (Task bus)
saying a container ran, from any other runner, or lost, for a dispatch nobody redeemedrefused
whose task_id is no dispatch of its keyrefused
the late ending of a dispatch its key was requeued pastno news: the requeue owes its own ending, which the same host gives from its record if the requeue comes back to it
delivered twicewritten once: the stream drops a copy from the same runner, task_id and state within two minutes, and the controller reads a known ending as no news
Decision

A result is heard only from the runner its dispatch is bound to: otherwise any machine of a pool could settle any task of the pool, and a compromised host would reach beyond the tasks in its hands.

A task's running and publishing travel on the same subject as $defs/taskProgress, told apart from a result by its progress keyword where a result carries state, and heard from the same runner as the result (Task states).

published by the runner as the container starts, and again with publishing as it exits
{ "task_id": "01JMZ8V1PC7K3M0", "idempotency_key": "01JMZ8V1P9C4/invoice/2/3/8",
  "runner": "runner-dmz-02", "progress": "running" }

A result's usage is sampled from the daemon's statistics while the container runs: one sample as it starts, then one per collection, about a second apart.

usageIs
cpu_secondsThe last processor total read.
max_rss_bytesThe highest memory any sample saw, less the page cache the container stopped using, as docker stats shows it.
image_pull_ms0 only where the host already held the image, in a result whose container started; a result that ran no container, a pull the deadline cut short included, carries no usage.

The first two are what the samples saw: time spent after the last sample, and a peak between two samples, are not counted. They are read off the same samples and travel together or not at all, so a container that exited before its first sample reports neither. image_pull_ms is always there once a container started.

Heartbeat

  • A runner posts one heartbeat every 10 seconds to the API, listing the idempotency keys it currently holds and those whose result it has not yet published, since a finished task would otherwise be declared lost while its result waits. One request covers every in-flight task on that host. It keeps alive only the dispatches of those keys bound to that runner, since after a requeue one key can also name a dispatch on another host. A restarted runner also names, from its first heartbeat until each is published, the key of every result it rebuilt from the record (Task bus).
  • Liveness therefore lives in the database beside the task state, rather than as traffic on a work queue that exists to distribute work.
  • The heartbeat is also how a drain or a revocation takes effect and how the console knows a runner is present: there is no separate liveness channel to keep in sync.
The request carriesMeaning
runnerThe identifier the join answered. One naming another runner than its credential's is refused with 403 and nothing of it is recorded.
agent_versionThe agent now running, which after the join only the heartbeat can say.
stateready, draining or unhealthy: what the runner will do with new work. Recorded for the inventory and never obeyed; the installation's own word is the runner's state.
concurrencyAGK_RUNNER_CONCURRENCY, reported every time since a restart is not a new join.
tasksEvery key held, at most 4,096; [] on an idle host.
sent_atThe runner's clock, never used to decide liveness, only compared with received_at.
The answer carriesMeaning
received_atAlways: the installation's clock, so a runner knows how far it has drifted from the clock its deadlines were written against.
drain: trueTake nothing new; finish what is held. Set by a drain and by a revocation (Registering a runner). While it is set the runner reports draining, and a message it was already being handed is put back at once, before it is redeemed, for another runner of the pool; one whose key an earlier agent on this host held is redeemed, since it may be bound here, and one whose redemption was already asked is refused with 403 and put back.
results_accepted_untilThe end of a revocation's grace, or the rotate_by of the credential the heartbeat carried where that comes first, since a revoked runner rotates nothing.
reasonWhy the runner is drained, only beside drain: true.
cancelEach key the request named whose dispatch, bound to this runner, the controller has ended as cancelled or timed_out. Never a lost dispatch: a host only cut off finishes its key (Task bus). A key already stopped through agentiik.stops is not stopped again, and one the runner no longer holds is passed over.
Decision

A stop travels on both channels with one meaning. agentiik.stops is the fast path and keeps nothing; the heartbeat's cancel is the backstop, so a runner disconnected when a stop went out hears it within one interval rather than running the container to its deadline.

A key is held from the moment the runner writes it down on the host, through a redemption asked again, the run and the publication of its result, until the bus has taken the result. A restarted runner also names, from its first heartbeat and for one AckWait (a minute), every key its record says an earlier process took and never ended: those it had redeemed are bound to it, their containers perhaps still running, and a message it never acknowledged comes round within that minute to be taken again. Past it, a key nothing brings back is let go of: its task is declared lost 30 seconds later and requeued, and the requeue, likeliest to come back to this host, adopts the container by its label. A key the wire's grammar refuses is left out and logged rather than sent, since the API refuses a heartbeat naming one whole.

Three missed intervals, 30 seconds, move a redeemed task to lost. The controller's sweep moves them before it decides anything, so the runs a loss wakes are decided on the same pass (see Lifecycle and replay).

A task in flightLost
redeemed30 seconds after its runner's last heartbeat naming it, or after its redemption until one does
not redeemed: on the queue, or taken and not yet redeemednever: the bus still holds its message, since a runner acknowledges only once it has redeemed, and its deadline is what ends it (see Task bus)

Registering a runner

Registration proves which pool an unknown machine belongs to, and gives it credentials worth having only on that machine.

  1. An administrator creates a runner pool with its labels, its accepted namespaces and its resource ceilings, then issues a join token: single use, short lived (one hour by default), bound both to that pool and to the exact set of labels a runner may claim with it. Every installation starts with one pool, default, carrying no label, accepting every namespace and setting no ceiling: it is where a step naming no label goes.
  2. On the host, as root: agk-runner join --api https://agentiik.example.com --token agkjoin_… --labels zone=dmz,arch=amd64. It generates an Ed25519 keypair for the private key at /var/lib/agentiik/runner.key (mode 0600, owned by the agent's account, agentiik unless --user names another), and sends the public key, the labels it claims (--labels or AGK_RUNNER_LABELS, or none, where neither is given, which is what a runner of the pool default claims: a token of default permits no label, and such a runner takes the steps that name no runs_on. A runner claiming no label in any other pool runs nothing, since every step sent there names a label, and join says so), its AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES, its capacity as measured on the host (vCPU, MemTotal, and the disk available under AGK_RUNNER_WORKDIR), its architecture, its agent version and its containment as the daemon reports it. Nothing is written until the API answers, so a refused token leaves nothing behind, key included. The private key never leaves the machine.
  3. The API verifies the token, checks that the claimed labels are a subset of what the token permits and that any namespaces the host narrows itself to are ones its pool accepts, refuses anything else, creates the runner record and returns a runner identifier, the pool, and a credential shown once and valid until its rotate_by. The identifier is minted as a lowercase ULID, the grammar results, bus subjects and URLs read it in.
  4. The credential goes to /etc/agentiik/runner.env, mode 0600, owned by the agent's account, beside AGK_API, AGK_RUNNER_ID, AGK_RUNNER_POOL, AGK_RUNNER_LABELS (only where it claims labels) and AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES, which agk-runner serve reads. The join token is spent. A host that has joined joins again only with --replace, as a new runner with a new key; the old one stays registered until an administrator revokes it. join also removes /var/lib/agentiik/credential, which belongs to the runner it replaces. A host whose runner.env remains without its key is told that it is a new runner.
  5. Every API call then carries that credential. The runner asks the API for a short-lived bus token at three quarters of its life, on a second connection that is listened on for stops before anything moves onto it; the connection it replaces stays open for bus.AckWait past its last take, and no longer than its credential, so nothing taken on it loses its acknowledgement. Bus credentials are therefore never at rest on a runner host, which is what lets a runner sit in a zone where a stolen disk must not yield a working queue consumer.
  6. The runner announces its labels and capacity, starts heartbeating, and pulls from its pool's queue.

A runner configured by its environment at every start, as a Compose file configures it, is given the join token too, in AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKEN or the file AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKEN_FILE names, and serve joins by itself:

At a start of serve given a join tokenIt
The host has no identityJoins, waiting up to five minutes for an API that does not answer yet, since a runner started beside its installation is often up before the API.
The key or runner.env is goneJoins again, as a new runner.
AGK_API, AGK_RUNNER_LABELS or AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES differ from what it joined withJoins again, as a new runner. The address is compared without its trailing slashes and the lists as sets, and one unset claims none.
Its environment claims what it joined withServes, and leaves the token unused.

The runner it was stays registered until an administrator revokes it: the API checked the address and the labels against the token when they were claimed, so an identity cannot follow a change to them, and a runner serving as one its environment no longer describes would be serving under claims nobody checked. Without a token, such a difference refuses the start.

Decision

A step goes to one pool, never several: a pool is a queue, and a task on two queues would run twice. A runs_on that is empty goes to default. A pool whose labels are all carried by another is reached only by a step naming none of the other's extra labels: with dmz labelled zone=dmz and dmz-gpu labelled zone=dmz,gpu=true, runs_on: [zone=dmz] matches both and fails. Give each pool a label of its own.

Afterwards

EventWhat happensWhy
restartIdentity is the keypair on disk, and serve carries the credential it last renewed to, from /var/lib/agentiik/credential, in preference to runner.env. A host whose key is gone, or is not an Ed25519 key, exits 3 before any call and joins again as a new runner.Nothing to re-register: the private key never left the machine, so the runner that comes back is provably the one that joined.
reimaged hostA new runner, which joins again, as is any host whose key is gone; one whose runner.env remains joins with --replace. The old record stays for the audit log.Never silently reused.
rotationAutomatic, as below: at two thirds of the window, and at the agent's first start for the credential join wrote, whose window the agent is never told. A credential past its rotate_by is refused everywhere, and that host joins again.A machine dark for a month should be reconsidered, not readmitted.
drain, revocationEffective at the next heartbeat, as below.Revoking a credential never destroys work already done.
labelsA runner claims only labels its join token allowed, and a token permits only labels its pool carries. A replacing join claims the labels it is given, never those of the runner.env it replaces, and serve refuses AGK_RUNNER_LABELS in its environment when the runner joined claiming none.The chain ends at an administrator, so a machine cannot add zone=lan to itself and start receiving the steps that were kept off the internet.
namespacesAGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES narrows the pool's list and never widens it. A namespace the pool does not accept refuses the whole registration, with the answer every bad token gets.A machine asking for more than it may have is one somebody should look at, and one answer for every refusal tells nobody which tokens exist.

Rotation

The key proves the machine: a stolen credential without it cannot be renewed.

at two thirds of the window
> POST /api/v1/runners/rotate                  # the current credential
{ "runner": "runner-dmz-02", "at": "2026-10-20T06:00:00Z",
  "signature": "…" }       # Ed25519 by runner.key, over "agentiik runner rotation", the runner and at, one per line

{ "credential": "agkrunner_…", "rotate_by": "2026-11-19T06:00:00Z" }
RuleWhy
rotate_by moves to now plus the join rotation, 30 days by default (Configuration)The window is rotate_by itself: nothing else to keep in step.
the signature is over the bytes agentiik runner rotation, a line feed, runner, a line feed and at, each as the request writes it, in standard base64The first line keeps a signature made for this from ever reading as one made for something else; the time is signed as written, so nobody has to agree on one spelling of it.
at is within five minutes of the API's clock, and later than the last rotation'sA copy of a signed request, from a proxy's log or a disk, rotates nothing, now or later.
the old credential also stops at its own rotate_byRotating is not a way for the old one to live longer.
refused: another runner in the body 403, a signature by any other key 403, at out of the window 400, at not after the last rotation's 409, a credential past its rotate_by 401A host whose key is gone is a new runner, and joins again.
a bus credential expires no later than the runner credential it was asked for withPast rotate_by, nothing the credential minted still pulls work. One minted with the old credential before the new one is used still lasts its hour: a bus credential cannot be withdrawn, as with revocation.
the old credential works until the new one is first usedA lost answer locks nobody out.
the new one is written to /var/lib/agentiik/credential, which serve prefers to runner.envThe unit's ProtectSystem=strict leaves /etc/agentiik read-only to the agent.
