the runner keeps the new credential on disk, mode 0600, before any call carries it, and switches to it at once; a 401 for a credential replaced on its way is sent once moreThe API stops taking the old one the first time it sees the new one.
a renewal with no answer is asked again with the old credential and a later at, from 1 s doubling to 30 sA lost answer locks nobody out.
a 401 exits 3; a 403 is a revocation if the heartbeat says so within two intervals, and renewing stops; otherwise the key is not the one the runner joined with, and it exits 3The API refuses a revoked runner's rotation before the next heartbeat tells it.

Drain and revocation

POST /api/v1/runners/{runner}/drain and /revoke take a reason and require grant:manage at installation scope; the audit log records both, in the transaction of the order.

DrainedRevoked, in its graceRevoked, after it
statedrainingrevokedrevoked
heartbeat answersdrain: truedrain: true, results_accepted_until401, as every call
resultsacceptedaccepted and recordedrefused; the sweep declares lost what is still held
bus credentialunchangednarrowed to publishing results and hearing stops, no pull; minted to last no later than the gracenone
a redemption403 for a task it does not hold, binds nothing403 for a task it does not hold, binds nothing401
log shippingacceptedaccepted401
rotationrotates403401
the agenttakes nothing new, finishes what it holds, stays up, idle, reporting drainingtakes nothing new, finishes what it holds, exits 3 once it holds nothing and every kept result is publishedexits 3 at the 401, as for a refused credential

Who ordered each is kept on the runner for the inventory, and recorded in the audit log; an order given again is recorded as unchanged. The grace's end is fixed at the revocation, so changing AGK_REVOCATION_GRACE afterwards moves no grace already given. A drain of a revoked runner is refused, and a revocation's reason replaces the drain's in the heartbeat.

The grace ends at the revocation plus revocation_grace, an installation setting defaulting to the task ceiling, one hour. That covers every step that writes no timeout, but not one that writes a longer one: a task still running when the grace ends has its result refused and is declared lost, coming back only as Back to pending says. An installation whose steps run longer raises the grace.

Open question

Whether revocation_grace should instead default to the latest deadline among the tasks the runner holds when it is revoked, so that no task a revoked runner already holds loses its result. The one-hour default stands until that is decided.

§

Lifecycle and replay

Task states

A task ends in exactly one ending, and the step's retry policy and the run's verdict are read from which one.

StateMeaning
pendingDecided and not yet handed to a runner.
dispatchedHanded out: on its pool's queue, or taken by a runner that may be redeeming it, pulling the image or running pre_task. Its deadline is the deadline the message carries, fixed when the controller dispatched it, so the wait on the queue, the redemption, the pull and pre_task all count against it. The grant expires at that deadline, and so do the URLs and the upload policy its redemption answered; a task nobody has redeemed by then is ended as Task bus says.
runningThe container is running.
publishingThe container is finished; its outputs are being collected and uploaded. A state of its own because the result is not yet safe, and losing a runner here is not losing one mid-run.
succeededThe container exited 0 and its envelopes were published.
failedThe container exited non-zero. Which failure it is, and whether it is worth another attempt, is read off the exit code and nowhere else. See Exit codes.
lostThe runner that redeemed it stopped reporting. A loss of a task already stopped as superseded or sibling_failed while its run goes on stays on the task's row, so the heartbeat's cancel never names it, and wakes nothing: the task ended when its stop went out.
timed_outStopped at its deadline, or ended by its run's root timeout: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period. Not failed, because the brick decided nothing and a retry written for transient failures should not answer a deadline.
cancelledStopped, or called off before it started, because the run was cancelled by a principal, by a concurrency group, by a merge: first or by fail_fast. Not failed for the same reason, and not timed_out because somebody changed their mind rather than a limit firing.
Decision

A task has one deadline, fixed when it is dispatched, rather than one that starts when its container is created. The grant, its URLs and the upload policy expire with it, and a deadline that started later would leave a container running past the credential it posts its outputs with. The cost: a full queue, a slow pull or a slow hook spends the step's time, so a timeout has to cover them.

Decision

running and publishing reach the tasks table as $defs/taskProgress, which the runner holding the task publishes on its own results subject as the container starts and as it exits (The task message). Progress is for reading a run and never for deciding one: the evaluator is not told, and it carries no instant, since the ending carries the span.

A progress messageIs
for the dispatch its task_id names, from the runner that dispatch is bound to, moving the row forwardswritten
late, delivered twice, or behind what the row already saysno news
over an ending, or on a run that has endednever written
from any other runnerrefused
ahead of the dispatch being recordedcomes round again, by when it is

A decision of the controller never moves a row back to dispatched.

Back to pending

EndingComes back whenKeytask_idretry.maxBackoff
failed, timed_outthe retry policy accepts the failure, read off the exit code for failed and as timeout for timed_out, and retry.max leaves an attemptnew: attempt + 1newuses onebase, doubling, never past max; none if unset
lostretry.on names lost, the step is idempotent, and the key has gone out again fewer than max_requeues timesthe samenewuses nonenone: due at once
max_requeuesIs
set byThe installation, as AGK_MAX_REQUEUES on the controller (Configuration). Never the workflow file.
values3 where the installation sets nothing; 0 requeues nothing; a negative number is refused.
countedPer key, one for each loss, which is a runner the control plane stopped hearing from. A message handed to another runner after AckWait, or a task waiting on a full pool's queue, spends none. A further attempt is a new key and starts again at none.
past itThe loss stands. The task stays lost, no retry.max attempt is spent, and the step fails on the infrastructure's account, its reason naming max_requeues.
Decision

A loss uses up no retry.max attempt: it is charged to the infrastructure, and a brick that never failed has spent nothing. Nor does it wait out a backoff, which spaces attempts so that a dependency can recover: what failed is the host, and going back on the queue leaves it behind.

So max_requeues is what bounds a loss, and it is the installation's: without it, a step whose container takes down every host it lands on is requeued until the run's timeout, and for ever without one. An author who could raise it would be spending somebody else's fleet.

Run states

StateMeaning
queuedCreated, waiting on a concurrency lock or on namespace quota.
runningAt least one task active or ready.
waitingSuspended at a wait step, for a duration, an external signal or a human approval; nothing else puts a run here. The state a mobile notification is meant to clear.
succeededEvery reached step finished, none failed beyond tolerance. A task not over when the run ends, which can only be one of a step a merge: first superseded, is written cancelled in the pass that ends the run, and every redeemed one is stopped with reason superseded, repeated in the heartbeat's cancel. Its runner's report later adds the exit code its container exited with, its log and its usage, and nothing else.
failedAt least one step failed without continue_on_error. A task not over is ended as for succeeded.
cancelledCancelled by a principal holding workflow:run, by a concurrency group, by a merge: first, or, from v0.3.0, by the controller when its principal fails the check at creation (Sessions and tokens). The one state a run can end in without having started, when it is cancelled from queued.
timed_outThe deadline set by the root timeout of the entry point expired. Every task not over is written timed_out in the pass that ends the run, and every redeemed one is stopped with reason deadline, repeated in the heartbeat's cancel. Its runner's report later adds the exit code its container exited with, its log and its usage, and nothing else.

Memoisation and replay

cache and idempotent, on two steps
steps:
  summarise:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/agk-summary@sha256:3b7a10...e4d2
    cache: true         # same image, parameters and inputs: republish, start nothing
  send-receipts:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/agk-mailer@sha256:c90e52...71fa
    idempotent: false   # never cached, never requeued after loss
  • Cache key. The digest of the image digest, the resolved parameters and the input envelope digests concatenated, prefixed by the namespace. A hit republishes the same envelopes without starting a container. It never crosses a namespace boundary.
  • Replay from a step. Reuses the envelopes and artifacts already produced upstream; content addressing guarantees nothing is rewritten. Once they have expired, the run replays only from the beginning, and a cache entry pointing at an expired artifact is not a hit. See How long an artifact lives.
  • idempotent. A step declared idempotent: false is excluded from the cache and from requeue after loss. The default is true, which puts the burden on the brick author.
§

Security model

Who the adversaries are, what stops each one, and what stops none. The mechanisms live in Isolation and secrets, Identity and access control and Component communication.

AdversaryAfterWhat stands in the way
A workflow author in one namespaceAnother namespace's secrets, artifacts or run dataDeny by default. Secrets referenceable only from their own namespace, and declared only at its own paths. Artifacts namespaced: read through presigned URLs scoped to one run, written under a policy that reaches only the task's own namespace. Cache keys prefixed by namespace. No secret value in any task message.
A brick image, hostile or compromisedThe host, its other containers, the networkA non-root user, no daemon socket, and the settings applied to every container, user-namespace remapping and a network per task included.
A compromised runner hostThe installationIt holds no database credential, no secret-store credential and no standing object-store credential. Only a runner credential and per-task grants that expire. Its reach is the tasks in its hands and the namespaces its policy accepts, and on MinIO or S3 the objects of those tasks' namespaces too (below).
A phisher, or a stolen passwordA working sign-inA passkey is bound to a Relying Party Identifier and the browser checks the origin, so a look-alike site gets nothing usable. With passwords forbidden, no shared secret is left to steal, phish or replay.
A page on another host of the same siteActing with a signed-in browser's sessionSameSite=Lax keeps another site's page from carrying the cookie on a request that changes something, but a browser counts every host under one registrable domain as the same site. So a request carrying a session changes something only where its Origin header is the public URL's, and the cookie's __Host- prefix keeps any other host from setting one the API would read.
An unauthenticated callerAnythingDeny by default; webhooks authenticated per trigger; an inaccessible workflow answering the same 404 as an absent one, so that probing yields nothing.
A caller with a narrow grantMore than they holdAtomic permissions, a union recomputed per request, a deny that wins at any scope, and MCP tools they cannot use absent from the listing rather than refused on call.
An administratorRun payloads across namespacesNo implicit run:read_data anywhere. Widening their own access is a distinct action, audited and told to the namespace's owner.
The supply chainEvery runner at onceDigests, signatures, published provenance and SBOM, and rebuilds: see Supply chain.
A compromised control-plane nodeEverythingNothing sufficient: see below.
Decision

workflow:write is arbitrary code execution. A workflow names images and commands, so whoever can push runs code of their choosing on that namespace's runners: that is the product, not a flaw. Grant it like commit access to a running service; the container and the runner pool contain it. Authors not trusted that far get a pool of their own, with a sandboxed runtime.

Three tiers of containment

TierWhat runs the containerWhen
hardenedThe default runtime with the container settings, plus user-namespace remapping, so container root is an unprivileged host account. In Docker's words: "If a process attempts to escalate privilege outside of the namespace, the process is running as an unprivileged high-number UID on the host, which does not even map to a real user."Every installation, always. The runner refuses a daemon without the remapping, unless require_userns_remap = false is written in its configuration file for a development machine (Installing a runner).
sandboxedgVisor's runsc on a dedicated pool: a userspace kernel, written in a memory-safe language, intercepts system calls. Stronger isolation, at the cost of "reduced application compatibility and higher per-system call overhead", worst for system-call heavy work.A namespace running code its own owners will not vouch for.
separatedA dedicated runner pool on hosts of its own.The requirement is separation, not sandboxing, and no runtime setting satisfies it.

Remapping "introduces some configuration complexity in situations where the container needs access to resources on the Docker host, such as bind mounts", and every brick gets bind mounts under /agk. The runner therefore prepares each task's working directory with ownership inside the remapped range before it creates the container, so no operator has to.

Supply chain

  • Images by digest on a server: a tag is a mutable pointer, and a version must determine what ran. agk push resolves each reference to the registry digest the pushing daemon holds for it, the version records name@sha256, and every run of it runs the same bytes. A reference with no registry digest, built locally and never pushed, is refused at push, and a runner refuses a message whose image is not a digest.
  • Signatures checked against a per-namespace policy naming who may sign, by the runner before the container is created, not by the registry.
Pullingv0.2From v0.8.0
credentialsnone: registries every runner can reach. A 401 fails the task on the platform's account and names v0.8.0.namespace secrets, redeemed for the pull
signaturesnot verified: there is no policy to verify againstthe per-namespace policy, in the runner
  • The standard catalog publishes build provenance and targets SLSA Build Level 3: runs that cannot influence one another, and secrets out of reach of build steps, as this documentation demands of a run.
  • Each catalog image publishes an SBOM as an OCI referrer, so "are we affected" means reading an attestation, not unpacking a filesystem.
  • Catalog images are rebuilt on a schedule and on base-image advisories, and the catalog shows their age: an image not rebuilt is stale, not stable.

Secrets, honestly

Decision

A step handed a secret can exfiltrate it, whatever the secret store does. The only control that bites is egress, so egress is per step and default-deny: network: none by default, egress.allow naming hosts and ports, a runner proxy enforcing the list, as the worked example shows. The tmpfs mount, last-moment retrieval and masking only reduce incidental exposure.

  • Masking is a literal match against the values the task was given. A secret base64-encoded, URL-encoded, split across lines or hashed gets through. It is a guard against accident, never against intent.
  • The built-in store wraps per-secret data keys with a master key held outside the database, so a database dump alone yields nothing.
  • Rotation is a write. No role reads a secret value back through the API.
  • Revoking a grant does not protect a secret a step already used; rotation does. The console says so when the grant is revoked.

Webhooks

  • HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, per-trigger secret, constant-time comparison. The raw body, because two JSON encoders disagree on whitespace.
  • A signed timestamp, a five-minute window and a nonce cache covering it: a captured request cannot be replayed, inside the window or out.
  • Signature failures are counted per trigger and surfaced. A sudden run of them is an unannounced rotation or somebody guessing.

Two questions that come up

  • The image cache is shared between namespaces, and that is fine. Layers are cached by digest, and a digest is not a secret. The runner checks that the namespace may use the reference before starting anything, and private registry credentials are namespace secrets, so no namespace can cause a pull it is not entitled to. The credentials arrive in v0.8.0 and the check in v1.0.0; until then every registry is one every runner can reach.
  • The audit log is append-only and chained. Each entry carries the hash of the previous one, so an edit or a deletion leaves a break, not a silence. It is exported continuously outside the installation, since the incident's own host may be unreadable.

Cryptography in use

ForWhat
user authenticationWebAuthn Level 3 passkeys, user verification required by default (user_verification). Only the public key is stored, so nothing stolen from the server authenticates anyone.
passwords, where still allowedArgon2id at the OWASP baseline: 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations, 1 degree of parallelism.
TOTP, beside a passwordRFC 6238: HMAC-SHA-1, 30-second steps, 6 digits, one step either side of the server's clock, no code accepted twice; a 160-bit secret, sealed under the master key as a built-in secret value is, bound to its user and its identifier.
tokens, join tokens, grants256 bits of entropy, stored hashed, shown once, each with an expiry.
transportTLS 1.3 where both ends allow it, TLS 1.2 as the floor, no plaintext path anywhere, including between the control plane and the bus. A local unix socket, PostgreSQL's on its own host or the Docker daemon's, is not a path in this sense: it never leaves the machine and its file permission guards it. Nor is a loopback address, which agk, a runner's AGK_API and the addresses handed to a runner may use; AGK_BUS_URL and AGK_PUBLIC_URL take no such exception. The other exceptions are http to a trace collector over loopback (AGK_OTLP_ENDPOINT), and the hop from a TLS terminator to the API or the controller's metrics in plain HTTP, on a network only the terminator reaches, where AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE names no certificate.
artifacts, trees, imagesSHA-256, which also makes them addressable.
the built-in secret storeEnvelope encryption with AES-256-GCM data keys, wrapped by a master key held outside the database.
runner identityAn Ed25519 keypair generated on the host at join; the private half never leaves it, and signs each rotation.

What this does not defend against

GapWhat remains
A compromised control-plane nodeIt holds the database credential and the secret-store role, so it gets whatever the store would give. Scope that role to the namespaces in use, and rotate on suspicion rather than on schedule.
A malicious administratorConstrained and recorded, not prevented. The audit chain shows the actions afterwards.
A brick that mishandles its inputA brick that logs what it was given has logged it. The catalog is reviewed; a third-party brick is its author's responsibility.
A kernel exploit escaping a containerWhat the sandboxed tier and a separate pool are for, which makes the tier a real decision rather than a default.
Traffic analysisA network observer learns when runs happen and roughly how large they are.
Writes under an upload policy on MinIO or S3A runner holding any task of a namespace can overwrite any object of it. Reads check the digest, so the cost is availability, not integrity; what refuses the write is not decided.

Disclosure

  • A security policy in agentiik/.github, shared by every repository, naming a contact and a coordinated disclosure window.
  • Advisories against the affected repository, with an identifier where warranted. Each names the component, which decides whether an installation was exposed, and one fixed version, since every repository carries one version.
  • Catalog SBOMs let an operator answer an advisory about a dependency without waiting for one about Agentiik.
§

Isolation and secrets

Settings applied to every container

Built from the documented fields of HostConfig and the Resources struct it embeds.

FieldApplied value
NetworkModenone by default. egress is to attach a dedicated network whose outbound traffic goes through a runner proxy enforcing egress.allow, and is refused until that proxy exists. internal attaches a network with no outbound route and no address of the runner host in it, for steps that only talk to a sidecar service; it needs Docker 28.0 or later, and an older daemon refuses internal and still runs none. Every task gets its own network, so two containers on the same host never see each other.
ReadonlyRootfstrue. The only writable paths are /agk/out and /tmp. /tmp is a tmpfs sized by tmp_size in runner.toml. /agk/out is a bind of the task's working directory, held to inline_max_bytes, envelope_max_bytes and max_items as it is collected, and not a tmpfs, because a tmpfs is gone when the container stops, before collection.
CapDropALL. CapAdd is refused unless runner.toml allows it explicitly. No workflow or manifest can ask for a capability yet, so allow_cap_add is a permission nothing exercises.
SecurityOptno-new-privileges, the default seccomp profile, and an AppArmor profile or SELinux label depending on the host.
daemon: userns-remapOn every runner: root in a container is an unprivileged high-numbered host account. A daemon setting, not a container field, and the runner refuses to start without it (Three tiers of containment).
MemoryFrom resources.memory, capped by the pool's ceiling, which is also what a step asking for none gets, and by the namespace quota.
NanoCPUsFrom resources.cpu, capped by the pool's ceiling, which is also what a step asking for none gets.
PidsLimitFrom resources.pids, default 256, capped by the pool's ceiling, which is also what a step asking for none gets.
Tmpfs/tmp, with noexec,nosuid,nodev. The secret mount point /agk/secrets is a tmpfs volume of the task's own, read-only, noexec,nosuid,nodev: a tmpfs of the container's own is empty when it starts, so a container of the runner's, running the static helper, fills the volume and holds it until the task's container has started. The volume is removed with the task. /agk/out is a bind, as ReadonlyRootfs says.
Ulimitsnofile and nproc set in runner.toml.
AutoRemovefalse. The runner removes the container once logs and exit code are collected, so nothing is lost on a fast exit.
Open question

The egress proxy is v0.9.0 work, after a design section that settles: explicit or transparent, where it listens in each runner form, forbidden destinations, the grammar of a host, optional or mandatory, chaining to an upstream proxy, local runs, and how a refusal reaches the log. It must also keep a runner free of any inbound port.

Further rules

  • The daemon socket is never mounted inside a brick. A brick that builds an image goes through an unprivileged builder, run like any other brick.
  • The container user is non-root, required by the manifest and checked at publication.
  • Images by digest on a server, signatures verified by the runner before start from v0.8.0: see Supply chain.
  • The working directory of a task is created fresh, owned by an unprivileged account, and removed with the container, so no residue of one namespace survives into the next task on that host. What cannot be removed is said in the runner's log, naming the step, the task and the path; it does not change how the task ended. The run, step and attempt directories above it, shared by every task of that run, step or attempt, are swept once they have held nothing for an hour, and never sooner: on Docker Desktop a path removed and created again is refused as a bind source for about a second, which the next shard of the same step would hit.

Secrets

The namespace declares where each secret lives; a workflow only names the ones it uses. The worked example names billing and mounts it in its invoice step.

declared on finance, one secret per request
> PUT /api/v1/finance/secrets/billing                 # secret:write
{ "provider": "builtin", "value": "sk_live_…" }            # 201, and no answer ever returns it

> PUT /api/v1/finance/secrets/ledger
{ "provider": "env", "path": "AGK_DEV_FINANCE_LEDGER" }    # development only

> GET /api/v1/finance/secrets                         # workflow:read
{ "secrets": [
  { "name": "billing", "provider": "builtin", "mount": "/agk/secrets/billing",
    "declared_by": "alice", "declared_at": "2026-09-10T06:30:00Z" },
  { "name": "ledger", "provider": "env", "path": "AGK_DEV_FINANCE_LEDGER",
    "mount": "/agk/secrets/ledger", "declared_by": "alice", "declared_at": "2026-09-10T06:31:00Z" } ] }
named in agentiik.yaml
secrets: [billing]

steps:
  invoice:
    secrets: [billing]      # mounted at /agk/secrets/billing
providerHolds the value inpathRule
builtinThe installation's encrypted storenone: one is refusedThe value travels on the declaration's PUT as value, with encoding utf-8 (the default) or base64, and never back. A PUT without one keeps the value stored; rotating is writing again. Moving the declaration to another provider, or deleting it, destroys the value, and one holding none is refused at redemption rather than mounted empty.
envAn environment variable of the APIa variable name under the namespace's prefixDevelopment only: refused unless the installation opts in with AGK_ENV_PREFIXES (Configuration), giving the namespace a prefix that starts with AGK_DEV_, under which the API reads nothing of its own, and starts no other namespace's prefix. Checked at the PUT and again at every read. An unset or empty variable is refused at redemption.
vaultHashiCorp Vault, from v0.9.0a path under the namespace's prefixRefused at the PUT until then, since nothing gives a namespace a prefix in Vault yet.

AWS Secrets Manager, the store of the AWS profile, arrives in v0.9.0 beside Vault, under a provider identifier not yet named.

LimitWhy
a name on ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]*$, at most 255 charactersThe workflow names it so, and a step is given it in a file of that name.
a path of at most 1 KiBMore than a variable or a key needs, and every listing and Terraform plan prints it.
a value of 1 to 1,048,576 bytes once decoded, in a body of at most 2 MiBThe most the store seals; an empty value would be an empty credential file.
AnswerWhen
200, 201 with Location, 204a declaration read or changed, created, deleted
400a name, provider, path, value or encoding refused, an unknown field, or anything after the document
404no such declaration, or a namespace the caller may not see: one answer for both
413a body above 2 MiB or a value above 1 MiB
503a value sent to an installation with no built-in store attached; nothing is written

A redemption that finds no value fails the task and names the secret to the runner; why, the store's own answer, goes only to whoever runs the installation.

Decision

The namespace says where a value lives, not the workflow file: a path in agentiik.yaml would let anyone able to push aim a step at whatever the store holds, while a declaration sits behind secret:write and inside the namespace's own paths.

Here is where the value travels.

  • A secret belongs to a namespace. A workflow can name only secrets its own namespace declares, so moving it elsewhere breaks the reference rather than carrying access along. The push is to refuse an undeclared name from v0.4.0; until then the redemption refuses it, naming the secret, and the task ends with no container run (The task message).
  • Mounted at /agk/secrets/<name> on a tmpfs volume of the task's own, which no directory of the host names, never an environment variable by default, because a process environment is readable by its children and ends up in diagnostic dumps.
  • The runner obtains the value by redeeming at the API the per-task grant the controller issued for that one task and that one secret, before it acknowledges the message and pulls the image (Task bus), and writes it down only as the container is prepared. The API is the only component that opens a value; the controller names which secret a task may have and never sees its value. With builtin the controller's database connection can read the sealed rows, but holds no master key to open them.
  • Secret values are masked in collected logs by literal match against the values known to the task, before anything is written to the store. A redelivered task whose container is still running is masked with the values on its volume, which the container holds for as long as it runs, as well as with those of its own redemption. One limit: a redelivered task whose container has already exited has only its own redemption, given what the store holds by then, so after a rotation it masks the new value while the log may hold the old one, which reaches the store in clear. Whether a grant should keep the values its first redemption read is not decided.
  • Never reachable from condition expressions, only from params marked sensitive in the brick manifest.
  • No role reads a secret value through the API. Rotation is a write, never a read-then-write. Each write, and each removal, is recorded in the audit log with the declaration and whether a value was written, never the value.
§

Observability

SignalWhat it carries
tracesOpenTelemetry: one trace per run, one span per dispatch, its context handed to the container as TRACEPARENT (Environment variables) for bricks that use it. The namespace is a span attribute, so per-tenant latency is queryable. The controller exports each run's trace once the run has ended, over OTLP/HTTP JSON to AGK_OTLP_ENDPOINT; with none set, nothing is traced (Traces).
metricsQueue depth per runner label, task duration per brick and version, retry rate, loss rate, runner occupancy, end-to-end latency per workflow, exported by the controller in the Prometheus text format (Metrics). From v0.3.0, what each namespace holds against its quotas, and what the purges and the collection removed.
logsStructured JSON, indexed by run, step, attempt and shard, streamed live over SSE and archived in the object store. Reading them needs run:read; the payload viewer needs run:read_data.
envelopesEvery step keeps its input and output envelopes, readable as they are in the console and through GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/steps/{step}/outputs/{port} and GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/steps/{step}/inputs/{port}, so an incident is reproducible without extra instrumentation. What each dispatch was handed is kept per attempt and shard. Reading an envelope needs run:read_data; run:read sees the digests.
audit logSeparate and append-only. Sign-in success and failure, credential enrolment and removal, recovery codes issued and used, authentication policy changes, token creation and revocation, device registration, grant and deny changes, namespace and quota changes, manual trigger, approval, cancellation, secret write, runner policy change, runner drain and revocation, and any administrator action that widened their own access. What v0.2 records: Audit log.

A task's log is its container's standard error, masked on the runner and shipped to the API in chunks by POST /api/v1/tasks/logs while the container runs.

A task's logIs
shippedIn chunks while the container runs: every second, or at once when one is full (4,096 lines, 1 MiB). Standard error only, since standard output belongs to the result. A chunk with no answer is shipped again as it was, with the same seq, backing off from 1 s to 30 s; any other refusal ends the shipping. A runner reading truncated: true ships nothing more but the closing chunk.
closedBy the closing chunk, shipped once the container has exited and before the result is published. An API that does not answer it is asked again for three heartbeat intervals, 30 s, the silence after which the controller declares a runner's tasks lost. The result then carries the lines the API last said it holds, reported truncated, and no log where the API never answered. An agent stopped before the result was kept leaves it to be rebuilt, as the next row says.
resumedA dispatch carried again after its agent restarted goes on from where the API says the log stands, asked with a chunk past any gap, and is reported truncated, since what the container wrote while no agent read it is not there. A result rebuilt from the record after a restart addresses the log, reports it truncated and gives lines: 0, since the API's count went with the agent.
cappedWhere it is written, at the runner's own defaults for log_max_bytes and log_max_lines: 4 MiB and 50,000 lines, counting standard error alone, the runner's own lines on it included. Standard output belongs to the result, which envelope_max_bytes bounds, so an envelope written there never cuts the log short. A log the runner cut is reported truncated. Once capped, a chunk moves next_seq past itself, even past a gap, since nothing more is written.
storedOne object per chunk under <namespace>/logs/<run>/<task>/<task_id>/. The database keeps the index and never a line.
addressedagk://log/<run>/<idempotency key>, the key escaped as one path segment, which the result's log.uri copies from the API's answer.
past retentionGone: the step's stream answers 410.
unreadable, one chunkStreamed as a gap with its reason, and reported to the operator.

A step's log is read as one stream, GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/steps/{step}/logs, with every dispatch of the step in turn.

Decision

Dispatches are streamed one after another, never interleaved, so a position is one place in one log and a reconnect resumes exactly; in a fan-out only the earliest unfinished dispatch is live. A lost dispatch is let go at once, a cancelled or timed_out one is waited for up to 60 s for its closing chunk, and one never redeemed is let go once the step is over. A runner ships the closing chunk before it publishes the result, so a finished task's log is whole by the time its step is judged.

Traces

A traceIs
trace-idThe first 16 bytes of SHA-256 of the run identifier, so a run's trace can be found from the run alone.
the run's spanThe next 8 bytes of the same hash. Its attributes add agentiik.workflow, agentiik.commit and agentiik.trigger.
a task's spanThe first 8 bytes of SHA-256 of its task_id, or of its idempotency key on a local run. A child of the run's span, from the dispatch to the ending.
attributesagentiik.namespace, agentiik.run_id, agentiik.task_id, agentiik.idempotency_key, agentiik.step, agentiik.attempt, agentiik.shard, agentiik.requeue, agentiik.state, agentiik.runner, agentiik.exit_code.
Decision

The controller exports every span and no runner does: it decided every dispatch and heard every ending, a loss the heartbeat declared included, and it reads the namespace from the run's row rather than from whatever a runner says. Tracing is best effort: a collector that is down costs spans, never a decision, and a controller dying between ending a run and sending its trace sends none.

Audit log

The audit log is one chain across the installation, kept in PostgreSQL beside the act it records: an entry is appended in the act's own transaction, so an act that lands is recorded and one rolled back is not, and the audit log refusing an entry refuses the act. The database numbers, dates and hashes each entry after the last under a row lock, so acts committing at once take turns and never fork the chain. The application's role may only append and read, and triggers refuse a change, a removal or a truncation to every role.

WhatIn v0.2
an entryseq (from 1, no gap), at (the database's clock, written 2026-09-25T10:00:00.123456Z), actor, action, namespace (left out for an act on the installation), target, result (done, or unchanged for an act asked of something already so: a second cancellation, a runner drained twice), detail, prev_hash and hash (lowercase hexadecimal). On the wire detail is a JSON string holding the object's text, never a secret's value or a token: a receiver that re-encoded an object would reorder or respace the bytes that were hashed.
the hashSHA-256 over the bytes agentiik audit 1, the previous entry's 32-byte hash (32 zero bytes before the first), seq as eight bytes big-endian, then, in this order, at as written above, actor, action, namespace (empty where left out), target, result and detail, each as its UTF-8 length in four bytes big-endian followed by its UTF-8.
recordedrun.trigger, run.cancel, secret.write, secret.delete, namespace.create, namespace.delete, runner_pool.create, join_token.issue, runner.drain, runner.revoke. From v0.3.0, the identity and access events: user.create, user.delete, credential.enrol, credential.remove, enrolment.issue, enrolment.use, bootstrap.end, api_token.create, api_token.revoke, signin.succeed, signin.fail, policy.change, grant.create, grant.delete, namespace.update, and group.create, group.delete, group_member.add, group_member.remove, service_account.create, service_account.delete, since a group's membership changes what its grants reach and a service account is a principal that holds tokens. namespace.create, namespace.update and namespace.delete are acts on the installation and carry no namespace: namespace.create records the namespace as created and the owner's grant, which is also recorded as grant.create in the namespace, where whoever reads its log for who was given what finds it; namespace.update records the quotas as they then stand. api_token.create and api_token.revoke name the token by its identifier, never its value, and record whose it is, and at creation its expiry, label and scope, and for a token agk login minted, the credential that signed in: a service account's in its namespace, a user's on the installation. user.create and user.delete record the display name and whether an administrator; a user asked for again for a fresh link is recorded as user.create, unchanged, beside the enrolment.issue, which records the link's kind, its expiry and whether it replaced one. A user removed with their empty personal namespace is recorded as namespace.delete, personal, beside user.delete. group.create and group.delete record the members, group_member.add and group_member.remove the member, unchanged where nothing changed. grant.create and grant.delete are recorded in the namespace with the principal, the scope, the role or the permission denied and the expiry, and, where the namespace's owners were told, who was (notified); so do group_member.add, group_member.remove and group.delete, by namespace, where an administrator widened their own access by them. service_account.create and service_account.delete are recorded in the account's namespace, the removal with who created it; the built-in identity init or migrate gives a namespace from before v0.3.0 is recorded as service_account.create by installation, with built_in. signin.succeed is recorded by the account signed in, with the credential and the address. signin.fail is recorded by the address the sign-in came from, since nobody is signed in, with the reason, cut to 256 bytes: about the account a passkey names, or the credential ID as presented, cut to 64 characters, where it names none; the login a password sign-in named; or the account an enrolment link or a recovery code was issued for, or an unknown enrolment code where none of its value is kept, and never the code. The failures anybody can send, a passkey's before its signature verified, every password sign-in refused, and a code refused, whether presented to start a passkey's registration or to set a password, or a registration it started refused, append at most 10 entries from one address, an IPv6 address counted by its /64, and 100 from every address together, in a window of 10 minutes that each replica of the API counts for itself; past either a refusal is answered all the same, and the next entry says how many went unrecorded, so that the log never reads as if they had not happened. A refusal after the signature verified, a counter that did not move forward or a synced passkey where device_bound_only applies, is recorded whatever the bound says, since only whoever holds the passkey's private key can make one, and that is what the log is for. A user's first sign-in records namespace.create by installation and the owner's grant as grant.create in the new namespace. enrolment.issue by installation is agentiik-api recover's, naming the administrators told. bootstrap.end names the administrator and the credential that ended it. policy.change of the installation carries no namespace and targets installation; a namespace's is recorded in it; each records the policy as it was and as it stands, and, where passwords came to be forbidden, the logins whose password went and those suspended. credential.remove records the reason where the policy took a password: by its user where a passkey brought them to min_passkeys, by whoever changed the policy, after its policy.change, where the change came to forbid it, and by installation where a sign-in met one passwords are forbidden to; a TOTP generator going with its password is recorded beside it; credential.enrol records the suspension a passkey lifted, and for a password whether it replaced one and how many sessions that ended. run.cancel by installation is a run ended because its principal may no longer start it, with the principal, the workflow, the reason the run carries and the whole account (Sessions and tokens). Approval arrives with the wait step in v0.8.0.
not recordedWhat changes something and is no act of a principal the log is for, each route held to it by a test that fails when a route is added that records nothing and says no reason: a version pushed, whose row keeps who pushed it as its author; a TOTP generator started, which counts for nothing until its confirmation, which is recorded; a sign-out, since a session is no credential; a notification dismissed, a reader's copy of an act recorded already; a runner joining, whose join token's issue is recorded and which the inventory keeps with when it joined; a runner's own traffic under its credential, its heartbeats, rotations, redemptions, logs and bus credentials; an upload to /objects, under a URL or a policy its redemption signed; a request refused with 429; and a wrong guess from a signed-in session, a current password or a TOTP code, which is counted as a sign-in's is and not recorded.
the exportThe leading controller POSTs every entry, in order, as newline-delimited JSON (application/x-ndjson) to the https sink AGK_AUDIT_EXPORT_URL names, with the bearer token in AGK_AUDIT_EXPORT_TOKEN_FILE, within a second of its commit. HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY in the controller's environment are honoured, and a private authority is trusted through SSL_CERT_FILE. Delivery is at least once: a sink that was down is sent what it missed, and a receiver keeps one entry per seq. Nothing past a break is exported, and a redirect is not followed.
verifyingagentiik-api audit-verify FILE checks an export as its receiver wrote it, with no database, which is what the copy is for when the installation's own host is in question. The export itself checks each batch against the last entry the sink accepted, so an entry changed before it was sent stops the export there. At the start of each term the leading controller verifies the chain in the database from the last entry proved, recorded in audit_verified, and checks that record against the entry it names before trusting it. A break, or a record that disagrees, is a warning naming the entry, and holds the term up in nothing. Entries before the record are not read again: a change to one, as to an entry changed after it was sent, is found by comparing with the copy.
Decision

Why an https sink. It is the smallest thing that is both continuous and outside: every log collector and SIEM takes an HTTP input of this shape, it answers each batch so the export knows what arrived, and it leaves the host rather than landing on its disk. A file is a copy on the host in question, and syslog answers nothing to move a cursor on.

Decision

Why the check in the database carries on from a record rather than reading the whole chain. Reading it all would cost more with every act the installation ever recorded, and a failover is when a controller should lead soonest. The entries before the record are the exported copy's to vouch for, which is what the copy outside is for.

Metrics

The controller answers GET /metrics on AGK_METRICS_LISTEN, in the Prometheus text format, version 0.0.4, to a request bearing the token whose SHA-256 AGK_METRICS_TOKEN_FILE holds. Prometheus reads it as it is, and the OpenTelemetry Collector through its Prometheus receiver. Only the instance that leads reports a figure; a standby answers agentiik_controller_leading 0, so every instance can be scraped and a sum over them is the installation's figure.

FamilyTypeLabelsIs
agentiik_queue_depthgaugepoolTask messages on the pool's queue that no runner has acknowledged: waiting for a runner with room, or being redeemed.
agentiik_runner_pool_labelgaugepool, label1 for every label a pool carries, to read any pool figure per runner label.
agentiik_tasks_dispatched_totalcounterpoolDispatches handed to the pool's queue: first dispatches, further attempts and requeues.
agentiik_tasks_lost_totalcounterpoolDispatches declared lost, charged to the pool of the runner that held them. Over the dispatches, the loss rate.
agentiik_task_duration_secondshistogrambrick, version, stateHow long a container ran, start to end as its runner reported, by the brick and version its manifest declares, for an ending the controller takes as news. A container it had already stopped, as superseded or sibling_failed or by its run's ending, is not counted: the stop is what ended it. A script step has an empty brick.
agentiik_task_retries_totalcounterbrick, versionFurther attempts a retry policy granted after a failure or a loss that was not requeued. Over the durations' count, the retry rate; a retry after a loss has no duration beside it, since no ending came back.
agentiik_runner_slots, agentiik_runner_tasks, agentiik_runner_readygaugepool, runnerFor every runner heard from in the last three heartbeat intervals: the concurrency it reported, the dispatches bound to it and in flight, and 1 where it takes new work. Tasks over slots is its occupancy.
agentiik_run_duration_secondshistogramnamespace, workflow, stateA run's end-to-end latency, from its creation to its verdict, waits for its concurrency group and its quota included.
agentiik_controller_leadinggauge1 on the instance that leads, 0 on a standby.
agentiik_quota_used, agentiik_quota_limitgaugenamespace, quotaWhat a namespace holds against a quota, and the quota it sets, quota naming it by its identifier: the tasks in flight for max_concurrent_tasks, the runs created in the last 60 minutes for max_runs_per_hour, and the bytes of live artifacts and of writes under way for max_artifact_bytes. A quota the namespace does not set has no agentiik_quota_limit series. Used over limit, how full it is.
agentiik_artifacts_expired_totalcounterReferences past their retain the artifact purge retired, each lowering its object's count by one.
agentiik_runs_purged_totalcounterFinished runs past their retention whose envelopes the envelope purge let go of, published and handed alike. The run and its record stay.
agentiik_logs_purged_totalcounterTask logs past their run's retention deleted from the store whole. The line count stays.
agentiik_orphans_found_totalcounterFiles of the store that no row, no write under way and no envelope of a run under way named a day after they were written, handed to the collection: outputs of attempts that failed or were lost, and what v0.2 left. The collection counts them again as it deletes them.
agentiik_objects_collected_total, agentiik_objects_collected_bytes_totalcounterObjects the collection deleted from the store, and their bytes.
agentiik_metrics_folded_totalcountermetricObservations counted under _other because their family was full.
queue depth per runner label, and the loss rate per pool over five minutes
sum by (label) (agentiik_queue_depth * on (pool) group_right agentiik_runner_pool_label)
sum by (pool) (rate(agentiik_tasks_lost_total[5m])) / sum by (pool) (rate(agentiik_tasks_dispatched_total[5m]))

A counter or histogram keeps at most 1,000 label sets; one more is counted under the label set whose every value is _other, which no namespace, workflow, brick or pool can be named, and agentiik_metrics_folded_total names the family. The gauges are read at the scrape, so they hold the pools that exist and the runners heard from, and nothing that has gone. The two quota gauges keep 1,000 namespaces at each scrape, the first by name, and sum what the rest hold under namespace="_other" with quota kept as it is, since a sum of tasks and bytes would be no figure at all; agentiik_metrics_folded_total counts each reading so folded, at every scrape. Counters start at zero when a controller starts to lead, which a scraper reads as a reset; the purge counters carry no label and are written at zero from the start, so a rate over them holds from the first scrape.

Decision

The controller exports the metrics and the API none. It decides every dispatch, retry and loss and every verdict, holds the control plane's connection to the queues, and reads the runners from the database their heartbeats are written to; and exactly one instance of it leads, so a figure is reported once. Three API replicas reading the same database would report every gauge three times.

Decision

On a listener of its own and behind a token, never on the API's: the metrics name every namespace and workflow that ran and every runner, which a tenant must not read. The listener speaks plain HTTP, as AGK_LISTEN does, for a network only the monitoring reaches or a TLS terminator in front, or TLS itself where AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE and AGK_TLS_KEY_FILE name a certificate, the same pair the API reads.

§

API and command line

RouteEffect
Sign-in and identity
POST /api/v1/auth/passkey/optionsThe options of a ceremony, around a 32-byte challenge, single use and good for 5 minutes: an assertion's, naming nobody and asking user verification wherever any policy requires it; a registration's, for the user whose enrolment code the request carries, or whose session it carries, signed in within the last 10 minutes (The sign-in page). 403 from another origin, 409 on an installation addressed by an IP address, 401 for a code or a session that opens nothing, a code refused audited as signin.fail.
POST /api/v1/auth/passkey/verifyVerifies an assertion or an attestation against the challenge it answers, taken whatever follows. An assertion signs its account in, with a full session in the cookie, the counter and the Backup State recorded, and the personal namespace created at the first sign-in; one whose signature counter did not move forward is refused and its user told (Authentication). A registration records the passkey with its Backup Eligibility and Backup State flags; one an enrolment code started spends it and signs its user in, one a session started opens no other session. One 401 sentence for either refused, 403 naming device_bound_only for a synced passkey where it applies, from another origin, or for a registration from a session signed in more than 10 minutes before its options, and 409 on an installation addressed by an IP address. Audited as signin.succeed or signin.fail, and credential.enrol, enrolment.use and bootstrap.end as they apply. For a sign-in agk login started, carrying terminal, the answer carries redirect_to, its loopback address with a one-time code; a registration carrying terminal is a 400.
GET /auth/sign-in
GET /auth/enrol
GET /auth/assets/{name}		The API's own sign-in and enrolment page and its stylesheet and scripts, on the public URL's origin, to anybody (The sign-in page). The HTML is never cached and the files are revalidated by their ETag. An enrolment link carries its code after #, which a browser never sends, so the code reaches no access log. /auth/sign-in opened with a query other than agk login's, one redirect_uri on the loopback and one code_challenge, is a page saying so, 400, and never hands a code anywhere.
POST /api/v1/auth/sign-outEnds the session the request's cookie carries, from its next request, and clears the cookie: 204, and 204 again where it carries none, or one that opens nothing already, since the browser is signed out either way. From the public URL's origin alone, 403 otherwise, since a page of another host of the same site could otherwise sign a browser out; a bearer token is 400, a token being revoked at DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{id}. A session that may only enrol signs out as any other. Not audited: a session is no credential, and the sign-in that opened it is recorded.
POST /api/v1/auth/exchangeagk login's one-time code and verifier, answered with a 90-day API token of the account that signed in, labelled as agk asks, audited as api_token.create with the credential that signed in. The code is single use, good for a minute, and spent by the first exchange its schema accepts: one that opens nothing is one 401; one whose sign-in the policy now makes enrolment-only, whose password it now forbids, or whose synced passkey it now refuses, a 403; and a principal holding 100 live tokens a 409.
GET, PUT /api/v1/auth/policyThe installation's authentication policy, every setting written, read by any authenticated caller but a session that may only enrol, and as stored, never as an installation addressed by an IP address applies it. PUT is an administrator's, replaces it whole, a setting left out returning to its default, and is audited as policy.change; 409 naming the setting where it forbids passwords on an installation addressed by an IP address, or would leave no administrator able to sign in.
GET, PUT /api/v1/{ns}/auth/policyA namespace's tightening of it, its own settings alone, read by an administrator and by whoever holds a grant in the namespace. PUT is an administrator's, replaces it whole, {} tightening nothing, is refused with 409 naming a setting it would loosen, or as the installation's is, and is audited as policy.change in the namespace.
POST /api/v1/auth/loginPassword sign-in where the policy allows it, from the sign-in page's origin, with a TOTP code where the account holds a generator. Refused outright when passwords are forbidden, 403 naming the setting, not failed as a wrong password, and the account's password, where one is still stored, deleted then. Every other refusal of a sign-in from the page is one 401 with one sentence. Ten attempts for one login and thirty from one address in a sliding quarter of an hour, then 429 with Retry-After; a sign-in waiting five seconds for its turn to hash is 503. Where the policy requires a passkey, the session opened enrols passkeys and nothing else; an administrator's full session ends the bootstrap token where it lasts. For a sign-in agk login started, carrying terminal, the answer carries redirect_to, its loopback address with a one-time code, never beside a session that may only enrol. Audited as signin.succeed, and signin.fail for a 401 or a 403 by the policy.
POST /api/v1/auth/password/enrolA password set from the code of an enrolment link or a recovery code, on the enrolment page, where the policy that applies to the account allows passwords, as it always does on an installation addressed by an IP address. The code is spent, and the password opens the session a password opens, none for a suspended user: full, or enrolling passkeys and nothing else where the policy requires a passkey. An administrator's that opens a full session ends the bootstrap token where it lasts; where a passkey is required, their first passkey, registered from it, does. A recovery code replaces a password held, removes the TOTP generator beside it and ends the sessions the old one opened. 422 for a password that is the login. Audited as credential.enrol, enrolment.use and signin.succeed, and a code refused, or passwords forbidden to its account, as signin.fail.
PUT, DELETE /api/v1/me/passwordThe caller's password, set from a browser's session, one that may only enrol included: a first one takes a sign-in in the last 10 minutes, and a change the current one, which counts as a guess at it as a sign-in does, a wrong one answered 403; a change ends every other session the old password opened. Removed, with the TOTP generator beside it, from a full session, where the account holds as many passkeys the policy accepts as min_passkeys asks, and never on an installation addressed by an IP address, where it is the one credential that signs in: 409 otherwise, naming min_passkeys where it is the reason. A password is at least 12 characters and at most 1,024 bytes, and not the login, with no rule on what it is made of. Audited as credential.enrol and credential.remove.
POST /api/v1/me/totp
POST /api/v1/me/totp/confirm
DELETE /api/v1/me/totp		A TOTP generator beside the password, from a browser's full session signed in to in the last 10 minutes: started, its secret and its otpauth:// URI answered once, which the sign-in page shows as text and as a QR code; enrolled when a code it shows confirms it within ten minutes, and counting for nothing before; removed with a code it shows, which counts as a guess. 409 for an account holding no password, or a generator already. Audited as credential.enrol and credential.remove.
GET /api/v1/me/credentialsThe caller's credentials, oldest first, each with its identifier, type, and for a passkey its kind, flags and label, and when it was enrolled and last used; never a public key, a hash or a secret. A token narrowed by a scope reaches none.
DELETE /api/v1/me/credentials/{id}Removes one of the caller's credentials, by the identifier the listing shows, from a browser's session, and ends the sessions it opened. A passkey the policy accepts whose removal would leave fewer than min_passkeys, and the password where fewer are held, are refused with 409 naming it; so are the password on an installation addressed by an IP address, the last credential, and a TOTP generator, which is removed with a code it shows at DELETE /api/v1/me/totp. Audited as credential.remove.
POST /api/v1/users/{login}/enrolmentA new enrolment link for a user who holds no credential yet, single use and good for an hour, shown once with Cache-Control: no-store, revoking any earlier one. A user holding a credential already is refused with 409: a lost one is replaced with a recovery code. Administrator only, and the bootstrap token's until it ends, whose link for an administrator is a first administrator's (Enrolment links). Audited as enrolment.issue.
POST /api/v1/users/{login}/recoveryA recovery code authorising the enrolment of a passkey, or of a password where the policy allows passwords, and nothing else, single use and good for an hour, answered once with the link that carries it and revoking the user's open one. Issued whatever the user holds, and sent nowhere. Administrator only, never for the caller's own account (403), and the bootstrap token's until it ends, its codes ending with it. Audited as enrolment.issue with both identities.
POST /api/v1/auth/tokensAn API token for the caller or a service account of a namespace it owns (Administrators), shown once, with Cache-Control: no-store, and kept as its SHA-256. It expires after 90 days unless the request asks otherwise, and after a year at most, a minute past it taken as asked: an expiry already past or further away is refused with 422, as is a principal that is neither the caller nor such a service account, and a namespace's built-in NS/agentiik, for which none is minted. A token narrowed by a scope, the bootstrap token, and a service account's token asking for that same account mint none: 403 (Sessions and tokens). A principal holding 100 live tokens is refused another with 409. Audited as api_token.create, in the namespace of a service account's token.
GET /api/v1/auth/tokens
DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{id}		The caller's tokens and those of the service accounts of namespaces it owns that are still accepted, newest first, each with its expiry, last use, device label and scope, never a value; and the revocation of one, from its next request, audited as api_token.revoke. Revoking one already revoked answers 204 again and is recorded unchanged; one the caller may not revoke is answered the 404 of one that does not exist. A token narrowed by a scope lists and revokes itself alone.
GET /api/v1/meThe caller: its principal as written, whether it administers the installation through the credential it presented, its user or service account record, neither for the bootstrap token, and its groups; its effective permissions keyed by scope, each namespace where it holds anything and each workflow where a grant, a deny or the token's scope makes them other than its namespace's, narrowed by that scope; and its notifications, newest first: an administrator having written a grant in a namespace by the installation's power, or widened their own access there, told to its owners (Administrators), a sign-in refused for a passkey's signature counter, told to its user, and a recovery code agentiik-api recover issued an administrator, naming the account, told to every administrator (Authentication): admin_access_widened, passkey_counter_refused and break_glass_recovery. A token narrowed by a scope reads no notification, since reading what the installation tells a principal is none of the nine. What agk whoami prints.
DELETE /api/v1/me/notifications/{id}Dismisses one of the caller's notifications, 204, changing nothing the audit log recorded. One not the caller's, one dismissed already and one past its 90 days are the same 404, and a token narrowed by a scope dismisses none, as it reads none. One not dismissed is kept 90 days, and removed when its reader next reads GET /api/v1/me past them.
POST /api/v1/me/devicesA mobile device: platform, push token, label. Revoked with the API token it is bound to.
PUT /api/v1/me/notificationsNotification preferences, per namespace and per event kind.
Administration
POST /api/v1/namespacesA shared namespace, its owner and its quotas. The owner is required, a user or group:NAME, and is given the owner role on the namespace in the same transaction, so that it can share it and act in it from the start; the namespace's built-in NS/agentiik is created with it. allowed_runner_pools names pools that exist. A name a namespace or a login holds is refused with 409; an owner naming no user or group, or a pool that does not exist, with 422. Administrator only, audited as namespace.create, and the owner's grant as grant.create in the namespace.
GET /api/v1/namespacesThe namespaces the caller holds a grant in (Administrators) and its token reaches, and every one for an administrator through a token with no scope.
GET /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}One namespace: its kind, its owner where it has one, and its quotas. To an administrator and to a principal holding a grant in it (Administrators); anyone else is answered the 404 of one that does not exist. What Terraform refreshes and imports a namespace with.
DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}Removes a namespace that holds no workflow, run, secret, stored object or service account but its built-in NS/agentiik, which goes first; refused otherwise, saying what it holds, since what a namespace holds is somebody's work. Its grants and its authentication policy go with it. A user's personal namespace is refused with 409, since it is removed with its user. Administrator only, audited as namespace.delete.
GET, PUT /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/quotasThe namespace's quotas and allowed runner pools, read by whoever reads the namespace. PUT is an administrator's: it replaces the set whole, as Quotas per namespace says, refuses a pool that does not exist with 422, and is audited as namespace.update with the quotas as they then stand.
GET, POST /api/v1/usersThe users, by login; and a new one: login, display name, the login where none is given, and admin where it is an administrator. Created with no credential, and answered 201 with an enrolment link shown once, single use and good for an hour, with Cache-Control: no-store. Asked again for a user who has not enrolled, with nothing said otherwise than was recorded, it answers 200 with a fresh link and revokes the one before, a field left out keeping what is recorded, so that a link that lapsed unused locks nobody out. A user who has enrolled, one asked for again with another display name or admin, and a login a namespace holds are refused with 409; a login outside the namespace grammar, a reserved word, operator or installation, and a display name over 256 characters or holding a line break or another control character, with 400. Administrator only, and the bootstrap token's until it ends: an administrator it creates gets a first administrator's link, anybody else a new user's (Enrolment links). Audited as user.create, unchanged for a repeat, and enrolment.issue.
GET /api/v1/users/{login}One user: login, display name, whether an administrator, whether suspended, when created and last signed in; never a credential. Administrator only. What Terraform refreshes and imports a user with.
DELETE /api/v1/users/{login}Removes a user with their credentials, tokens, sessions, enrolment links, memberships, grants and notifications, and their personal namespace where it holds nothing, recorded as namespace.delete beside user.delete. Refused with 409, naming it, while their personal namespace holds something or another namespace's record names them as owner, so that no work is lost with them and no namespace is left owned by somebody who is gone; and, once the bootstrap token has ended, for the last administrator who can sign in (Administrators). Administrator only, audited as user.delete.
GET, POST /api/v1/groupsThe groups, each with its members by login; and a new one, empty or with up to 1,024 first members. A name outside the namespace grammar, or a member named twice or no login can be, is refused with 400, a member no user is with 422, and a name a group holds with 409. Administrator only, a creation audited as group.create with its members.
GET /api/v1/groups/{group}One group and its members. Administrator only. What Terraform refreshes and imports a group with.
DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group}Removes a group with its memberships and grants, what they gave its members ending from their next request; its members stay. Refused with 409 while a namespace's record names it as owner. An administrator removing a group they are in tells the owners of each namespace where its denies took a permission from them (Administrators). Administrator only, audited as group.delete with its members, and who was told.
PUT, DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group}/members/{login}Adds or removes one member, touching no grant: the member gains or loses what the group's grants give from their next request, since grants are resolved from memberships at every request. Answered with the group as it now stands; adding a member already in, or removing one not in, answers the same and is recorded unchanged. A group that is not there, a login no user can have, and adding a login no user holds are 404, saying which. An administrator putting themselves in, or taking themselves out, tells the owners of each namespace where that widens their own access (Administrators). Administrator only, audited as group_member.add and group_member.remove with the member, and who was told.
GET, POST /api/v1/service-accountsThe service accounts of the namespaces the caller owns (Administrators), each namespace's built-in NS/agentiik among them, by namespace and name, each with who created it and when; and a new one in one of them, {namespace, name}, written NS/NAME from then on, holding no grant and no token. A name outside the namespace grammar, or agentiik, is refused with 400; a namespace the caller does not own, and any through a token narrowed by a scope, which owns none, with 422; a name the namespace holds with 409. A creation is audited as service_account.create in the namespace. Tokens via /api/v1/auth/tokens.
DELETE /api/v1/service-accounts/{ns}/{name}Removes one of a namespace the caller owns, with its tokens and its grants, from the next request they would have made; audited as service_account.delete in the namespace, with who created it. The built-in NS/agentiik, which goes only with its namespace, and one a namespace's record names as owner, are refused with 409; one that is not there, or not of a namespace the caller owns, is the same 404.
POST /api/v1/runnersJoins a machine to the pool its join token names, with its public key, labels, capacity, architecture and agent version, and its namespaces and containment where it sends them. Answers the runner identifier, the pool, a credential shown once and its rotate_by. Authenticated by the join token in the body alone. See Registering a runner.
GET /api/v1/runnersRunner inventory: labels, capacity, last heartbeat, the state and concurrency it last reported, who drained or revoked it and when, and the end of a revocation's grace. Administrator only.
POST /api/v1/runners/{runner}/drain
POST /api/v1/runners/{runner}/revoke		Drains or revokes one runner. The body is {"reason"}, one line of at most 256 characters, handed to the runner at its next heartbeat. Answers the runner as GET /api/v1/runners lists it, with drained_by, drained_at, revoked_by, revoked_at and results_accepted_until. 404 for a runner not there, 409 for draining a revoked one. An order given twice keeps the first, so revoking again adds no time. Requires grant:manage at installation scope. See Registering a runner.
POST /api/v1/runners/rotateA runner's new credential and its rotate_by, for its current one and a signature by its key over the runner and at. Runner credential only.
POST /api/v1/runners/heartbeatEvery 10 s: runner, agent_version, state, concurrency, tasks and sent_at, answered with received_at, drain, cancel, and reason beside a drain. Another runner's name is refused with 403. Runner credential only. See Heartbeat.
POST /api/v1/bus/tokenA bus credential for the caller's own pool, which it reads from the runner credential, lasting no longer than an hour, the credential's rotate_by and a revocation's grace: pull from the pool's consumer, publish results on its own subject, hear agentiik.stops, and no pull once revoked. Runner credential only.
GET /api/v1/runner-poolsPools and their labels, to write a namespace's allowed pools against. Administrator only.
POST /api/v1/runner-poolsA pool with its labels, accepted namespaces and resource ceilings. Administrator only. The pool's consumer is created in the same step: a bus that refuses it answers 503, and no pool is created.
POST /api/v1/runner-pools/{pool}/join-tokensA join token: single use, short lived, only for labels the pool carries, shown once. Administrator only.
POST /api/v1/tasks/redeemA task's grant, redeemed by a runner for the tree and input URLs, the secret values and one upload policy, the first answer binding the task to it. Answered from what the controller wrote beside the grant and never from the request: see The task message.
POST /api/v1/tasks/logsOne chunk of a task's masked standard error, from the runner the task is bound to, with the task's grant in the Agentiik-Grant header and never in the body: idempotency_key, seq, first_line, final and lines. Answered with the log's uri, accepted, next_seq, lines and truncated. Chunks are taken in order: one shipped again is answered as held, one past a gap is answered with next_seq naming the gap and kept nowhere, and the last closes the log. A draining runner, and a revoked one in its grace, ship the logs of the tasks they hold. Runner credential only. See Observability.
GET, PUT /objects/{key...}
POST /objects/{ns}		The built-in object store, where a presigned URL or a signed POST policy is the whole authorisation and every object is held to its digest: see The task message. A write is held to its namespace's max_artifact_bytes, refused with 507 where it would take the namespace past it, and holds its object against the collection from before its bytes are read.
Namespaces, workflows and the catalog
GET /api/v1/{ns}/secrets{"secrets": [...]}, each declaration with name, provider, path where it has one, mount, declared_by and declared_at, never a value. Requires workflow:read at namespace scope.
GET /api/v1/{ns}/secrets/{name}One declaration, the same way.
PUT, DELETE /api/v1/{ns}/secrets/{name}Declares, changes or deletes one secret: provider, path, and for builtin a value no answer returns. One secret per request, so two Terraform applies never drop each other's change. Requires secret:write at namespace scope. See Secrets.
GET /api/v1/{ns}/grantsThe grants and denies written on the namespace, which every workflow in it inherits, leaving out those expired: each with its identifier, principal, scope, role or denied permission, expiry, and who granted it and when. Requires grant:manage on the namespace.
POST /api/v1/{ns}/grantsShares the namespace: principal as written, a role or a deny naming one permission, optional expiry, at the scope the path names and never one the body could. A grant binding neither a role nor a deny, or both, is refused with 400; an expiry already past, a principal that names nobody, and a service account of a namespace the caller does not see, answered alike, with 422. Requires grant:manage at namespace scope, or an administrator through a token with no scope, whose grant, as any widening of their own access, is told to the namespace's owners (Administrators). Audited as grant.create in the namespace.
DELETE /api/v1/{ns}/grants/{id}Revokes one grant or deny written on the namespace, from the next request, and for every run not yet let in. One written on a workflow is revoked at the workflow's route, and answered here as one not there, 404. Requires grant:manage on the namespace. Audited as grant.delete; a deny taken from an administrator's own access is told to the owners as a grant is.
GET /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}/grantsThe grants and denies that apply to the workflow, leaving out those expired: its namespace's first, then those written on it, each with its scope, so that what it inherits is told from what is written on it. Requires grant:manage on the workflow.
POST /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}/grantsShares the workflow, as the namespace's route shares the namespace. Requires grant:manage on the workflow, or an administrator, as there.
DELETE /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}/grants/{id}Revokes one grant or deny written on the workflow, from the next request, and for every run not yet let in; one written on its namespace is answered 404 here. An open log stream asks again every 30 s, credential and run:read, and ends once either is gone.
POST /api/v1/{ns}/workflowsAn empty workflow repository, with default branch and protection settings.
GET /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}Default branch head, resolved graph at that commit, commit history.
GET, POST /{ns}/{name}.git/*Git smart HTTP. Clone and fetch need workflow:read, push needs workflow:write, and secret:use in the namespace where a commit names a secret; a pre-receive hook validates the entry point before any ref moves.
GET /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}/tree/{ref}The tree at a ref, for the console and for review.
PUT /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}/versions/{commit}Registers a commit as a version: its entry point, its includes and the files of its tree, refused if the graph cannot be built from them. A PUT because a commit pushed twice with the same files is one version; with other files it is refused with 409, since a commit names one tree. A tree above the limits is refused with 413. Refused with 422, before any tree is stored, where an input's schema does not compile against the pushed tree, names a file it does not carry, or weighs more than 128 KiB in all, a file counted once per input naming it. Refused with 403, before any tree is stored, where the version names a secret and the caller holds no secret:use in the namespace (Permissions). What agk push sends until git hosting arrives. Requires workflow:write.
GET /api/v1/bricks, /bricks/{name}The catalog, and a brick's manifest with its parameter schema, to discover what exists before writing a workflow. Any authenticated principal.
Runs and their data
POST /api/v1/{ns}/workflows/{name}/runsManual trigger: a commit pushed as a version, and the workflow inputs, bound against that version's declaration as agk run --local binds them and recorded as bound (Workflow inputs). A ref other than the default branch arrives with git hosting. Example below. Requires workflow:run.
GET /api/v1/runsThe runs of every workflow the caller holds run:read on, over its namespace or itself, newest first, each with its namespace. Where a mobile app opens. Narrowed by namespace, workflow, state, since and until (RFC 3339, on when the run was created, both included) and limit (50 by default, at most 500). A namespace the caller cannot read lists what one that does not exist lists. Also served within one namespace as GET /api/v1/{ns}/runs. Within one namespace, each workflow is asked about in turn, so a namespace the caller holds nothing in lists nothing.
GET /api/v1/runs/{id}Run state, per-step state, envelope digests, each task with the digests it was handed on its input ports, and its namespace; and each task with its exit_code wherever its ending carries one, a stopped container's included. Its inputs are envelope contents: answered only to a caller holding run:read_data on the run's workflow, and otherwise left out, as for a run started with none. Its reason, where nothing in its workflow ended it, says why, as for a run refused when it was let in (Sessions and tokens). Requires run:read on the run's workflow. The same answer as GET /api/v1/{ns}/runs/{id}, the path a Location names a run by.
POST /api/v1/runs/{id}/cancelAsks for the run to be cancelled, and the controller carries it out: 202, example below. Requires workflow:run on the run's workflow.
POST /api/v1/runs/{id}/approveClears a waiting run. Optional comment, audited. With the wait step, in v0.8.0.
POST /api/v1/runs/{id}/rejectEnds a waiting run as cancelled, with a reason. With the wait step, in v0.8.0.
POST /api/v1/runs/{id}/replayReplays from a named step, reusing everything upstream.
GET /api/v1/runs/{id}/steps/{step}/logsSSE log stream of every dispatch of the step, in the order they were made, each its history then what its runner ships. Events dispatch {task_id, idempotency_key, attempt, shard, requeue}, line {task_id, line, at, text}, gap {task_id, first_line, lines, reason}, dispatch_end {task_id, lines, truncated, final}, end {verdict}.
