Light or dark follows the terminal's background: at start the console asks the terminal for it with the OSC 11 query Lip Gloss sends, and takes the light palette on a light background. A terminal that has not answered within a tenth of a second is taken as dark, as most are, and AGENTIIK_THEME, light or dark, settles it for a terminal that never answers, as some multiplexers never do.

StateDark groundLight ground256, dark256, light16 colours
running#4FBFAC, the accent's hue#0E6A5F3723cyan
succeeded#5FA773#2E7D4F7229green
waiting#D9A441#96660A17994yellow
failed, timed_out#E0705A#B23C1E16788red
queued, skipped, cancelled#6D7B73, faint#7E8C84243245the terminal's faint

As in the colour rules, no state is its colour alone: each is a word beside a dot, a spinner or a ring, and a shard strip adds position, which is why NO_COLOR loses nothing.

Decision

The console draws in the palette's own values, where this chapter first chose the terminal's sixteen colours. The sixteen read well on the ground they were chosen for, but they are a different red and a different green in every terminal, so the console would look like any other tool and not like the product whose web console a person already reads. The palette's values read on the palette's grounds, which the console paints under what it draws, and asking the terminal for its background picks the ground that suits it. The sixteen remain where a terminal offers no more, which is where their argument still holds.

Where it runs

WhereWhat it does
a terminal, local or over SSHDraws on the terminal's alternate screen and hands the screen back as it found it on exit, an interrupt included. Needs 80 columns and 24 rows, what a terminal opens at, and lays out more where there is more (Panes and layout). No browser, no local port.
over SSHThe keys and the mouse work as locally. SSH does not carry COLORTERM unless its configuration sends it, so a true colour terminal usually draws in 256 colours there; SendEnv COLORTERM on the client and AcceptEnv COLORTERM on the server bring the exact palette back.
a machine with no browserTakes its token in AGENTIIK_TOKEN, made elsewhere with agk token create, since agk login needs a browser beside agk for its loopback redirect (Authentication). On a host others use, a token narrowed with --scope opens only what it names.
NO_COLOR set and not emptyNo colour at all. Nothing is lost, since every state is a word.
standard input or output not a terminal, or TERM=dumbNo screen. The view it would have opened is printed once as plain lines, and it exits 0, so a script or a cron job never waits on a screen nobody sees. The runs view is one line per run, columns separated by tabs, no header, times in RFC 3339; a run is what agk status prints; a graph is the list above.
not a terminal: the runs view as lines
$ agk console --namespace finance | grep ^failed
failed	01JMZ8V1P9C4QX7T2N5R8WD3HK	finance/monthly-invoicing	manual	2026-09-27T05:41:03Z	1m 52s	alice

What it leaves to the web console

Left to the web consoleWhy
editing a workflow, in the graph or in its fileEditing is review and commit, and at a terminal the clone, the editor and git are already there. An editor inside agk would be the format-preserving one written a second time.
the repository browser and the diff of two commitsgit does both in the clone.
starting a run with inputsA form drawn from a JSON Schema is a browser's. agk run --namespace takes the inputs from a file and follows the run, which appears in the runs view as it starts.
passkeys and the credentials viewSigning in and enrolling are ceremonies a browser runs, which is why agk login hands its sign-in to one; the credentials they make are managed where they are made.
fetching an artifact, or any payload written to diskA host reached over SSH is often shared, and a payload left there is business data on a machine nobody audits. Envelopes are shown on screen, and a step's files listed by name, media type, size and digest.
changing grants, and what an administrator managesThe console shows sharing and runners and changes neither, as the decision below says.
the brick catalog and the MCP panelReference, read while writing a workflow, with the links and rendered schemas a browser gives.
the statistics and their chartsA chart zoomed with the mouse, read under the pointer and exported is a browser's. The terminal draws the compact form of the same series, a sparkline and a histogram (Statistics).
Decision

The terminal console acts on runs and nothing else: cancel, replay from a step, and from v0.8.0 approve and reject, the moves of somebody watching runs at three in the morning. A key pressed in a list is a lighter act than a line typed, and a grant, a user or a quota deserves the sentence agk share, agk user and agk namespace make a person write, which a script can repeat and a review can read. Dismissing one of the principal's own notifications is the one other thing it does, since it changes nothing anybody else sees.

§

Mobile applications

The phone answers one question: is anything wrong, and can I unblock it from here? Authoring stays on the desktop. Both applications are native, share no code, and use the same authorised HTTP API as every other client.

Common scope

FeatureWhat it covers
sign-inA passkey through the platform's own credential APIs, against the same Relying Party Identifier as the console. One or several installations, a token for each.
run listFiltered by namespace, workflow and state, with the failing and waiting runs surfaced first.
run detailThe per-step state, timings, the step that failed, its exit code and the tail of its log.
approvalApprove or reject a waiting run, with a comment, which is what clears waiting.
run actionsCancel, replay from the failed step, or start a manual run from saved input presets.
notificationsOn failure, on an approval request, and on completion of a run the recipient started. Preferences per namespace and per event kind.
graphRead-only, to find the step an alert names.

What the applications do not do

  • Edit or register a workflow. Editing is review and commit, and belongs where the repository is.
  • Show envelope payloads or download artifacts without run:read_data, or ever write them to disk.
  • Store credentials outside the platform keystore, or keep a payload in the offline cache, which holds run metadata only.

Platform choices

ItemiOSAndroid
languageSwift, SwiftUIKotlin, Jetpack Compose
targetsiPhone and iPad, one universal appphone and tablet, one app
token storageKeychain, device-only, no iCloud syncKeystore-backed encrypted preferences
pushAPNsFirebase Cloud Messaging
live updatesSSE while the app is in the foreground, push when it is not
biometricsOptional local unlock before approving or cancelling a run
Decision

A push message carries an identifier and a state, never a payload, a log line or a workflow name, and the detail is fetched over the API on tap. A revoked grant then takes effect between the alert and the screen, and no business data transits through APNs or Firebase.

§

Public site

A statically generated site, deployed from its own repository: the front door and the documentation home. No account, no tracking, no third-party script: HTML, CSS and its own assets.

PageWhat it holds
homeWhat the product is, in one screen, with a complete workflow file readable without scrolling.
installThe Compose stack, the first administrator, the first workflow.
documentationThe brick contract and the operations guide, written by hand. The language reference and the API reference, generated from agentiik/schemas so that the site, the command line and the MCP tools can never teach three different languages.
brick catalogBuilt from the manifests of the standard bricks, parameters and ports rendered from their schemas.
release notesPer version: which components actually moved, and the API version the release speaks. No compatibility matrix, because the console, the command line and the applications of a release are that release.

Every version's documentation is kept. Versioning gives the addresses and how the default is chosen at publication.

  • The version selector sits in the header of every page and reads a list the site publishes beside them. On a page opened straight from a clone, with no list to fetch, it shows the one version there is and offers no menu.
  • The selector groups the two kinds of finished release apart: stable keeps its promises, release is a tagged 0.y.z that makes none.
§

Brick catalog

The standard catalog covers what recurs in every workflow, and no brick in it is more than a deterministic tool.

BrickRole
http-requestOne HTTP request per item, with authentication, timeout and retry policy.
jqItem transformation and filtering through a jq expression.
sql-queryPostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite query, with rows turned into items.
s3Object read, write and listing, with conversion to artifacts.
smtp-sendMail delivery with a template and attachments taken from artifacts.
imap-fetchMailbox polling, one item per message, attachments as artifacts.
csv / xlsxConversion between tables and items, both ways.
templateText template rendering per item, output as an artifact or as a field.
split / aggregateSplitting one item into several, or grouping items by key.
schema-validateItem validation against a schema, routing invalid ones to a dedicated port.
waitWaits for a duration, an external signal or a human approval, without occupying a runner.
execA command in an arbitrary image, under the standard input and output contract. A step written with script resolves to this brick.

Registry

  • Bricks are published to an ordinary OCI registry. The catalog is an index of the manifests and annotations read off it, with no parallel store.
  • A private installation points its catalog at its own registry.
  • A namespace may also declare private registry credentials. They are namespace secrets like any other, and never appear in a workflow shared with another team.
§

Storage

TableContents
principalsOne row per user, group and service account, keyed by the string that names it, alice, group:team-finance or finance/nightly-sync, which is what a grant refers to, so that a grant binds any of them without a special case. Removing one removes the user, group or service account it is, and all it holds.
usersLogin, display name, whether an administrator, whether suspended, when created, last sign-in, and the opaque handle the user's passkeys are registered under: random rather than the login, since an authenticator keeps it and WebAuthn asks that it name nobody. No credential material, and no mail, since the product sends none. Why the policy suspended an account where it did: for holding no passkey when passwords were forbidden, which a passkey enrolled from a link or a recovery code lifts.
credentialsOne row per credential, of one type, with the user's label and last use. A passkey keeps its credential ID, unique across the installation, its COSE public key as the authenticator sent it, its signature counter, its AAGUID, and its Backup Eligibility and Backup State flags; a password its hash, in the hasher's self-describing form, parameters included, so that a later cost still reads an older hash; a TOTP its secret, sealed under the master key, since a code is checked against the secret itself, and the step its last code was accepted at, so that no code is accepted twice. One password and one TOTP per user at most, and a TOTP only beside a password: removing the password removes it. A password set anew keeps its row and identifier, recorded as set then. The AAGUID is stored as received: under attestation conveyance none (Authentication) a client passes it on unchanged, so it may name the authenticator's model, and nothing certifies that it does. A password, where one still exists, is a row like any other, deleted rather than blanked.
totp_enrolmentsA TOTP generator started and not confirmed: its user, the identifier it will be enrolled under, its secret sealed as credentials will hold it, when it was started and an expiry ten minutes on. One per user, replaced by starting again; the confirmation moves it to credentials, and until then it signs nobody in and asks no sign-in for a code.
groups, group_membersGroup definitions and their membership.
service_accountsNon-human principals of one namespace, each with who created it, and the namespace's built-in identity, NS/agentiik, which nobody did. A namespace is not removed while it holds one but its built-in identity.
api_tokensHashed token, principal (a user or a service account, never a group), scope, device label, expiry within the year, last use, revocation.
sessionsBrowser sessions, hashed: the user, the credential that opened each, issue time, idle expiry and revocation. The idle expiry moves as the session is used, written once it moves by a minute, and never past 30 days from the issue. Removed with the user or the credential.
webauthn_challengesA challenge the passkey options issued: its 32 bytes, the ceremony, for a registration the user it enrols and the enrolment code that let it start, and when it was issued, with an expiry 5 minutes on. Taken, and removed, by the verification that answers it; those past their minutes are removed as others are issued. The code is held here and not spent, so that a ceremony dismissed halfway does not burn the link; removed with the user or the code.
enrolment_codesThe enrolment links of the three kinds, hashed: the user, the kind, who issued it (operator for the bootstrap token, installation for agentiik-api recover), when, an expiry within the hour, and when it was used or revoked. One open per user and kind, and one first administrator's link across the installation. A link opens nothing once its user holds a credential, and a recovery code the bootstrap token issued nothing once the token has ended: read so at each use rather than written as a revocation.
exchange_codesagk login's one-time codes, hashed: the user and the credential that signed in, the PKCE challenge, and an expiry within the minute. Taken, and removed, by the first exchange that presents one; removed with the user or the credential, and those a password minted when that password is set anew; those past their minute swept as others are minted.
devicesMobile registrations: platform, push token, label, bound API token, last seen.
notification_prefsPer principal, per namespace, per event kind.
notificationsWhat the installation tells one principal of its own accord, read in their GET /api/v1/me: its kind, when, and what it is about, the namespace and the grant as written, the passkey, or the administrator a recovery code was issued for, by login, kept whole rather than referred to since any of them may be gone before it is read. One row per reader, a user or a service account, never a group, whose members are each written one. Kept 90 days, removed on read past them or when dismissed, and removed with its reader or its namespace.
namespacesName, kind (personal or shared), owner (a personal namespace's user, the user or group an administrator names for a shared one, and none for one from before v0.3.0 or made by agentiik-api namespace create), quotas, allowed runner pools.
grantsPrincipal, scope (NS or NS/workflow), a role or the one permission denied, expiry, who granted it (operator for the bootstrap token) and when. Removed with its principal, its workflow or its namespace.
auth_policyThe authentication policy: one row for the installation, every setting written and never removed, and one per namespace holding only what it tightens.
bootstrapOne row: the bootstrap token's SHA-256, which init or migrate writes from AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN, or migrate imports once from the file AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN_FILE names where a v0.2 installation upgraded without init kept it, and when the token ended (First run). From then on the hash is gone and is never written again, so a line left in .env brings nothing back.
workflowsName, namespace, default branch, labels.
workflow_refsThe ref database of every workflow repository: ref name, commit, protection, who moved it and when. Git objects live in the object store as packfiles.
workflow_versionsOne row per commit accepted on a branch: commit, parent, resolved graph, the manifest of its tree (path, sha256, size and mode per file, each file a counted object), author, timestamp.
triggersActive triggers per version, schedule state, last firing.
runsIdentifier, version, state, trigger, triggering principal, timestamps, workflow inputs as bound, defaults included, and outputs, when a cancellation was first asked for, and why the run ended where nothing in its workflow ended it, a run refused when it was let in for one. When its envelopes and logs expire, set once it finishes; when the envelope purge and the log purge were done with it, so that neither reads again a run it purged; and files_recorded, set at every decision a controller of v0.3.0 makes on the run, so that a finished run without it is one whose artifact files a v0.2 controller left unrecorded.
stepsPer-step state within a run, envelope digests for each port.
tasksOne row per dispatch: task_id, idempotency key, shard, attempt, state, runner, exit code. A requeue after loss adds a row under the same key, and at most one row of a key is anything but lost.
task_logs, task_log_chunks, task_log_objectsWhere each dispatch's log stands, the index to its chunks, and every object a log was written to, recorded before the write. Never a line.
task_grantsEvery grant a dispatch was published with, hashed, each redeemable until it expires: a task published again keeps the grant its first message carries, and the first redemption binds the task, and the input envelopes it names, by digest, size and count.
approvalsWaiting run, requested at, decided by, decision, comment.
secret_declarationsOne row per namespace and name: provider, path, who declared it and when. No column could hold a value.
secret_valuesFor builtin, the value sealed under its own data key, which a dump alone cannot open, and a version that only goes up, so a row put back from a backup is refused rather than reopened. A value is forgotten, never its row deleted.
artifactsOne row per reference: namespace, run, step, port, digest, size, media type and that reference's expiry, and the fetches held for transfers under way. A reference is live, expired or collected; one past its expiry is refused before any purge retires it.
artifact_objectsOne row per object a namespace's store holds: digest, size, media type, its count, when the count reached zero and when a collection claimed it. The count is of what holds the object: the live references naming it, the envelopes a run keeps, what each task was handed on its input ports, once per grant, and the files of each pushed version's tree, once per distinct digest. A file of the store no row names is an orphan, handed to the collection as a row counting nothing.
artifact_uploadsThe writes through /objects, recorded before their bytes are read: in every namespace, a hold on the object against the collection until a day after the policy or the URL it was written with expires, so that a result heard late still finds its bytes; and, where max_artifact_bytes is set, its room, at the most the object may be until its bytes are in and then at their size, until a quarter of an hour after that expiry. A refused write gives its rows back; the purge forgets the others once they lapse.
artifact_roomOne row per namespace setting max_artifact_bytes: what it holds as last counted, with the room made since, and when it was counted. A write adds its room under a lock on the row, and the whole count is taken again once it is a minute old, or before a write is refused on a count more than a second old, so that counting every live artifact is not what each write waits for.
runnersLabels, capacity, version, accepted namespaces, last heartbeat.
audit_log, audit_head, audit_export, audit_verifiedAppend-only, one chain across the installation: actor, action, namespace, target, result, detail, each entry numbered and carrying the hash of the one before it. The application's role may only insert and read. audit_head holds the last link, which only an append moves, audit_export how far the sink has accepted the log, and audit_verified how far the leading controller has verified the chain, with that entry's hash; both only move forward.

Envelopes and logs are not stored in the database: it keeps only their digests and URIs. Object keys are prefixed by namespace, and every query path carries the namespace so that a missing filter fails closed rather than returning another tenant's rows. Retention is declared per workflow within the namespace ceiling, with separate purges for envelopes, artifacts and logs, and garbage collection of objects whose count reaches zero, run by the controller that leads from v0.3.0. How long an artifact lives sets out what is declared.

What each purge acts on

Three purges, three clocks, because the three things do not expire for the same reason. Collection follows from them and has no clock of its own, and the orphan sweep finds what nothing counts.

WhatDate set byResolved whenEffect
artifactsretain on the output that produced it, or defaults.retain, capped by max_retention_days, which is the date where neither is writtenthe reference is written; for a file living by defaults.retain, again when the run finishes, to the run's date where that is laterthe reference is retired, and the count falls by one
envelopesdefaults.retain, capped by max_retention_days, which is the date where the workflow declares nonethe run finishesthe counts on the run's envelopes, and on what its tasks were handed, fall by one each
logsas the envelopesthe run finishesthe log's objects are deleted, and the directories they leave empty, not decremented
orphansno date: a file of the store no row namesit is a day old, and no row, no write and no envelope of a run under way names ithanded to the collection, as a row counting nothing
collectionno date: it falls out of the othersthe count has sat at zero for the grace, 24 hours, no live artifact names the object and no write holds itthe object is deleted from the store
  • Envelopes and logs are not declared one at a time the way an output is, so they live by the workflow's defaults.retain, resolved to one date when the run finishes. A file living by the defaults, an intermediate's or a shard's, lives at least as long as the envelopes naming it, so that no envelope kept is read back naming bytes that are gone; an output declaring its own retain keeps the instant it declared.
  • The controller that leads runs them, and no other instance, so that two never delete the same bytes: one pass as its term begins and one every 10 minutes after, the artifact purge, the envelopes, the logs, the writes that lapsed, the recording of what v0.2 left, the orphan sweep, then the collection. Each call is one transaction over at most 1,000 rows, or 100 runs for the envelopes and the logs, called again while it comes back full and at most ten times a pass, the rest left to the next: a backlog, such as the months of expired rows an upgraded installation holds at its first pass, is worked through over as many passes as it takes and never holds a lock longer than one batch does. The lead is asked before every call, so a controller that lost it stops at the next call. A purge that fails stops no other, and the next pass takes it up again.
  • A pass that removed something says what in one line of the controller's log, the references, runs, logs, orphans, objects and bytes; one that recorded files v0.2 left says how many runs; and one that could not finish warns why. The metrics count the same.
  • Nothing waits on a pass. An artifact past its expiry is refused with 410 from that instant, whichever pass retires it, and max_artifact_bytes counts by the expiry, so a pass up to 10 minutes later changes nothing anybody reads; its bytes leave the disk a day after its count reached zero at the soonest. The schedule, the batches and the grace are constants rather than settings.
  • A write through /objects holds its object from before its bytes are read until a day after the policy or the URL it was written with expires, so that a result heard late, after the controller was down past the task's deadline, still finds its bytes; a refused write lets go at once. The deletion holds the rows it deletes the bytes of, and asks about writes only once it holds them, so a write and a deletion never cross.
  • A run v0.2 finished carries no expiry: migration 0038 gives it its namespace's max_retention_days from its end, the most any workflow could have declared, since the workflow's own defaults.retain was not recorded with the run, and keeping longer than asked costs disk where purging sooner would lose what was asked for. The files of its outputs given no retain, which v0.2 recorded nothing for, are recorded from its envelopes by init, by migrate given AGK_OBJECTS_DIR, and by the controller's passes, expiring at the same date.
  • The orphan sweep walks each namespace's sha256/ directory, a batch of entries a call, a round of the store taking as many passes as it needs. It never walks logs/, nor a namespace with a finished run whose files are still to be recorded, since those files are named by no row until they are. A namespace the database no longer holds, and a .staging- file a write left behind, are left for a later release.
  • Raising a namespace ceiling later extends no artifact: its date was decided when the reference was written.
  • A run that has not finished has nothing to purge: a purge acts on what has stopped changing. Ending a run that never finishes is the controller's job, not a sweep's.
  • An envelope is a counted object exactly like an artifact. What a task is handed on its input ports is counted too, once per grant, and the envelope purge drops those counts with the run's, so a fan-out's slices live exactly as long as their run. Two steps publishing identical bytes publish one object, so deleting by digest alone would delete what another step still names. A log is not counted: one task wrote it and nothing else names it.
  • What stays behind is the record: the digest of what was published, the line count of the log, the name, size and digest of the collected artifact.
Decision

An object is collected no sooner than a grace period after its count reaches zero, twenty-four hours, a constant rather than a setting. Content addressing lets a run writing the same bytes tomorrow reference the object already there; collecting at once would turn every such write back into an upload. Past the grace, a writer must send the bytes again, which closes the race with a sweep that has claimed the object but not yet deleted it. A shorter grace would shrink the store sooner and cost uploads.

Decision

An orphan goes two graces after it was written, not at once. A file is written before the row that names it, since a runner posts an output before the controller hears of the result, so one younger than a day may be a file whose row is about to be written. And a write that began before the orphan was handed over held nothing, there being no row to hold; a day later it has committed, and holds the object as any write does. Two days is what a file nobody names costs in disk; taking it sooner would risk the bytes of a result still on its way.

§

Deployment profiles

Every profile runs the same API, controller, console and runner images; it only decides where they run and what backs the database, bus, object store and secret store. The language, the brick contract and the access model never vary, so a workflow moves from a laptop to a redundant fleet unchanged.

What every profile must provide

RequirementWhy
Exactly one writable PostgreSQL, 18 in the Compose installation from v0.3.0, and 17 still on HomebrewLeader election is a session-level advisory lock: a second writable primary breaks the election rather than adding availability. The programs run on 17 and 18 alike; CI tests on 18.
A work queue with at-least-once delivery, one queue or subject per runner poolA runner pulls only from its own pool's queue, and a step reaches it by the pool's labels.
An object store every runner can reachArtifacts move by presigned URL and signed POST policy, never through the controller.
A secret store the API can read, and neither the controller nor the runners canSecrets. With builtin the sealed values sit in the PostgreSQL the controller shares, so the master key, held by the API alone, is what keeps them from it; a database role of the API's own is an open question.
An OCI registry every runner can pull from by digestSupply chain
TLS in front of the API and the console, terminated in front or served by the API itself (AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE)Passkeys need an HTTPS origin.
One Relying Party Identifier, chosen at installation and never changedChanging it invalidates every passkey, so the installer holds it immutable and offers re-enrolment instead. From v0.3.0 it is the host of the public URL, AGK_PUBLIC_URL or AGK_PROXY_URL behind a proxy, and every ceremony runs on the API's sign-in page, its one origin. The console arrives on the same origin, at the root of the public URL (Web console), so the identifier stays that host for good.
Nothing elseWorkflow repositories need no shared filesystem: objects sit in the object store, refs in the database.
ComponentSingle hostOn-premise, redundantAWS, managed
Failure domains13 racks, rooms or sites3 Availability Zones
APIone container3 nodes behind a virtual IPECS Fargate service across 3 AZs
Controllerone container3 nodes, one active by advisory lockFargate service, 2 tasks, one active
Consoleone containerserved by the same virtual IPS3 behind CloudFront, on the API's origin
Runner1, colocatedN hosts, pooled by labelEC2 Auto Scaling group
DatabasePostgreSQL containerprimary, synchronous standby, asynchronous replicaRDS PostgreSQL, Multi-AZ
BusJetStream, R1NATS cluster of 3, streams at R3SQS standard, one queue per pool
Object storeMinIO, single driveMinIO, erasure sets across the domainsS3
Secret storebuilt-in encrypted storeVault, 3-node RaftSecrets Manager
Registryany reachable registryinternal registry, signatures verifiedECR
TLSCaddy or Traefikterminated at the virtual IPterminated at the load balancer

Profile A: a single host

One machine, one Compose file: a homelab, a small team, or a developer reproducing an incident. No redundancy, on purpose: at this size a second copy of anything costs more attention than the outage it prevents.

The installation is the single-host directory of agentiik/deploy: Install a server shows its compose.yaml, and installs, operates, backs up and removes it. At v0.2.5 it runs PostgreSQL, NATS, the API, the controller and one runner, prepared by agentiik-api init at every start: the API serves TLS itself, objects sit on disk rather than in MinIO, and there is no console yet. From v0.3.0 PostgreSQL is 18, and postgres-upgrade upgrades the data of an installation that ran 17 before PostgreSQL starts, keeping the old cluster beside it.

The reverse proxy of the figure is optional: behind one, AGENTIIK_PROXY_URL sets AGK_PROXY_URL to the proxy's https URL and the API serves plain HTTP on the loopback, while the bus keeps its own TLS on 4222.

The images are published on ghcr.io from v0.2.1, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64: ghcr.io/agentiik/api, controller and runner, and postgres-upgrade from v0.3.0, tagged with the version (0.2.1 and v0.2.1) and latest at a release, and dev for every commit to main.

  • Secrets: the built-in store, with its master key read from a file the API user alone can open, or from the host keyring.
  • Backup: pg_dump and the data/ directory beside compose.yaml, restored together, or runs point at artifacts that no longer exist (the commands).
  • Upgrade: the whole installation stops together, which is acceptable at this size.

Profile B: on-premise, redundant

Three failure domains: racks, rooms or sites on a low-latency link. Stateful dependencies are replicated across them; stateless ones run in all three. Runners sit outside, in pools selected by label, because they hold no state worth protecting.

What happens when something fails

What failsWhat the installation does
a runnerIts tasks stop heartbeating and move to lost: requeued where the step is idempotent and its retry.on names lost, up to max_requeues times per key, surfaced for a human otherwise.
the active controllerIts session ends and the advisory lock is released; another node takes it and resumes from the database. Published tasks wait in the bus, untouched.
an API nodeThe load balancer drops it. A stopping API ends its log streams at once, without end, and readers reconnect elsewhere and resume with Last-Event-ID.
the PostgreSQL primaryThe synchronous standby is promoted; the controller reacquires its lock there, the same code path as a restart.
one NATS nodeR3 streams keep a majority. Nothing is noticed.
two NATS nodesQuorum is lost: nothing is dispatched and nothing is lost. Runs stay queued until a majority returns.
one object-store nodeReads and writes continue within the erasure set's parity budget.
a whole domainThe other two hold a majority for the bus and the database; the installation runs on with reduced headroom.
Decision

The controller runs active with standbys, never sharded. Sharding buys throughput the product does not need at this size, and loses the one place where the graph is evaluated: two instances could then publish the same task from two views of one run.

Profile C: AWS with managed resources

Every stateful dependency is a managed service; only the runners are instances someone owns.

Decision

The bus is SQS, not a self-managed NATS cluster, because the bus contract is narrow enough to substitute: standard queues "ensure at-least-once message delivery", a message leaves the queue when the consumer deletes it, and a long-poll receive is the runner's pull consumer. Given up: server-side subject filtering, hence one queue per runner pool, and stream replay, which WorkQueue retention never offered. Task messages carry no payload and sit far below the 1 MiB limit.

Decision

Runners are EC2 instances, not Fargate tasks. A runner drives a Docker daemon through its socket, and an ECS host bind mount (sourcePath) is "supported only when using tasks that are hosted on Amazon EC2 instances or Amazon ECS Managed Instances". The control plane mounts nothing and stays on Fargate.

  • An RDS Multi-AZ failover ends the session holding the advisory lock; the controller reacquires it as after a restart.
  • Per-pool egress is a security group plus a NAT with a filtered allow list, which enforces each step's egress.allow.
  • Each Auto Scaling group tracks its own queue's visible-message count: a fan-out of ten thousand items adds instances, and the run's tail gives them back.

Installing a runner

The commands, in order, are in Add a runner on another machine; this is what they rest on. Two forms, because the machines worth adding are not always machines anyone wants to run a container platform on.

FormWhenWhat it needs
containerAlongside the rest of a Compose or orchestrated installation. This is the single-host profile.The daemon socket; the work root mounted at the same path as on the host; the host's user namespace. The image starts as root: serve gives /var/lib/agentiik, the work root and /etc/agentiik to 65532, takes the group that owns the daemon socket, drops to 65532 and starts itself again so that its file capabilities apply. It never serves as root, and refuses the start where it cannot drop. The image carries the three capabilities below as file capabilities on agk-runner (setcap cap_chown,cap_fowner,cap_dac_override=ep), and cap_add: [CHOWN, FOWNER, DAC_OVERRIDE, SETUID, SETGID] keeps them in the bounding set, with the two the drop takes: without them the kernel refuses to exec agk-runner, since the file asks for capabilities the bounding set lacks. SETUID and SETGID are not file capabilities, so the agent that serves holds the three alone and cannot take root back. Nothing is prepared on the host: no group is named in the Compose file, and no directory is made first. The image holds the static helper of its own architecture at /usr/local/lib/agentiik/agk-helper; serve copies it to .bin/agk under the work root and binds that copy read-only at /agk/bin/agk for a script step, since the daemon resolves a bind's source on the host. /var/lib/agentiik and /etc/agentiik/runner.env are owned by 65532, the image's agentiik. Given AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKEN or AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKEN_FILE, serve joins on its own (Registering a runner); join remains for bare metal. Without labels, with a token of the pool default, the runner claims no label and takes the steps that name no runs_on. A private certificate authority is trusted through SSL_CERT_DIR, as the Compose files in agentiik/deploy hand it AGENTIIK_CA.
bare metalA physical host chosen for what it has: GPUs, a large local NVMe scratch, a specific kernel or driver, a licensed toolchain, or a position in a network zone.A single static binary run by a systemd unit, and the static helper of the same release at /usr/local/lib/agentiik/agk-helper; the binary runs as a user in the group that owns the daemon socket, holding the three capabilities below and no other; and a working directory on the fast disk.

Bare metal describes the agent, not the work: bricks are still containers, resolved by digest and started through the Docker Engine API. Only the agent is a process, so it survives a restart of the container platform it drives and can use host resources directly.

In either form, serve never serves as root: started as root, it drops to agentiik first (the container form). It refuses the start on a missing setting, an unreadable or malformed runner.toml, something other than a file at /usr/local/lib/agentiik/agk-helper, a daemon below its floors, a host whose memory cannot be read from /proc/meminfo, since a runner that cannot say how much it has cannot put back what it has no room for, a host key that is gone or not Ed25519 (exit 3), or a key or /var/lib/agentiik/credential that is unreadable, of the wrong mode or owner, or naming another runner, each before any call to the API. A missing runner.toml keeps every default, the floor included. Once the floor holds and the daemon is open, it posts its first heartbeat, and sends READY=1 over NOTIFY_SOCKET, which is what Type=notify waits for, once the API has answered it: a runner the API does not accept is not one to count as started. An API that does not answer is asked again, from one second doubling to ten. A 401 ends the start with exit status 3 and says to join again, and the unit's RestartPreventExitStatus=3 keeps systemd from starting it again, since a refused credential stays refused. A revoked runner exits 3 too, once it holds nothing and every result it kept is published, or at the 401 that ends its grace: a revocation is not undone, and joining again is the one way it serves again.

One runner setting is a floor, not a preference: require_userns_remap defaults to true, and a runner that finds a daemon without user-namespace remapping refuses to take work rather than start containers whose root maps to the host's. An operator who sets it to false has decided that this machine does not need the floor, which is a reasonable thing to decide about a laptop and a serious thing to decide about a fleet. It is a line in /etc/agentiik/runner.toml and not a command line flag, so the decision survives in something reviewable rather than in somebody's shell history. Three tiers of containment says what the remapping buys.

CapabilityLets the agent
CAP_CHOWNGive a task's directory to the base of the remapped range, before the container exists.
CAP_FOWNERRemove what a brick left in a directory it made sticky.
CAP_DAC_OVERRIDERe-enter and remove those directories when the task ends.
Decision

Three capabilities and no other. Membership of the group that owns the daemon socket is already root-equivalent, so they give an attacker nothing the socket does not, and without them the agent could not own a task's directory inside the remapped range. A task's secret values are on a tmpfs volume the daemon mounts from memory for that task alone, so the host prepares no tmpfs for them.

/etc/systemd/system/agentiik-runner.service
[Unit]
Description=Agentiik runner
After=network-online.target docker.service
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=notify
User=agentiik
# member of the group that owns the daemon socket, never root
SupplementaryGroups=docker
# AGK_API, AGK_RUNNER_LABELS and AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACES are in runner.env, which join wrote;
# repeated here, each must say the same, trailing slashes and list order aside, or serve refuses to start
Environment=AGK_RUNNER_CONCURRENCY=8
# reads /etc/agentiik/runner.env itself, so the credential stays out of the environment
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/agk-runner serve
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
# 3 is a credential the API refused, or a revoked runner done with what it held: joining again is the fix, and a restart is not
RestartPreventExitStatus=3

# three capabilities, to own a task's directory, and no other privilege
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_CHOWN CAP_FOWNER CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_CHOWN CAP_FOWNER CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/agentiik

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Each task running with network: internal holds a network of its own, taken from the daemon's default-address-pools, about 30 networks by default: a host running more such tasks at once needs larger pools. internal needs Docker 28.0 or later. The networks a runner left behind when it died are removed when the next one starts.

/etc/docker/daemon.json, room for 256 task networks
{ "default-address-pools": [{ "base": "10.200.0.0/16", "size": 24 }] }

Registration

  1. An administrator issues a join token: single use, short lived, scoped to a pool and the labels it may claim.
  2. agk-runner join --api https://agentiik.example.com --token <token> --labels zone=dmz,arch=amd64,gpu=true, as root, trades it for a credential in /etc/agentiik/runner.env, mode 0600, and a key in /var/lib/agentiik/runner.key, both owned by agentiik. A work root other than the default is best written as AGK_RUNNER_WORKDIR in runner.env before joining, which join keeps, so the disk it declares is the work root's.
  3. agk-runner serve announces the runner's labels, capacity and accepted namespaces, and pulls from its pool's queue. Draining or revoking it stops it taking work at its next heartbeat.

No inbound port is ever opened on a runner host; every connection is outbound, to the API, the bus, the object store and the registry. Full exchange: Registering a runner.

Runner-side hooks

Only the machine's owner can have the runner run commands on the host around each task, from /etc/agentiik/runner.toml, readable by the agent account alone. No workflow can set them, read them, or discover that they exist. They run from v0.9.0: until then the runner reads [hooks], runs none of them, and says so at start.

/etc/agentiik/runner.toml
[hooks]
timeout = "30s"

# before the container is created, after the image is resolved
pre_task = [
  "/usr/local/sbin/attach-licence --slot $AGK_TASK_ID",
  "nvidia-smi -L > /dev/null",
]

# after the container is destroyed, whatever the verdict
post_task = [
  "/usr/local/sbin/release-licence --slot $AGK_TASK_ID",
  "find $AGK_WORKDIR -mindepth 1 -delete",
]
  • Hooks receive AGK_TASK_ID, AGK_NAMESPACE, AGK_WORKFLOW, AGK_STEP, AGK_IMAGE and AGK_WORKDIR, and nothing else: never a secret, an envelope or a parameter.
  • A non-zero exit from pre_task fails the task as an infrastructure failure, charged to the runner and not to the brick. After a few consecutive ones the runner marks itself unhealthy, rather than failing a whole pool one task at a time.
Decision

Runner hooks and step scripts never share a shell. GitLab's pre_build_script "Runs in the same shell context as before_script, script, and post_build_script", so a job can read what the administrator's hook set up, and the reverse. Here they share only the workspace directory, as drawn above: a hook gives the workflow author a ready machine, never a variable.

Sizing

WhatSized by
runner concurrencyOne task per vCPU to start, raised until memory or disk queue binds rather than CPU. A runner puts back on the queue a task whose declared resources would exceed its own declared capacity, so oversubscription is a choice, not an accident.
control planeRun creation rate and open log streams, never the data volume of workflows: it holds state, not payloads. Its bandwidth follows the rate at which steps publish, not the size of what they publish.
databaseRun and task history, bounded by retention.
object storeArtifacts, which only a retention policy bounds.
Decision

A task's declared resources are the cpu and memory on its task message, after the pool's ceilings; a part the task leaves out counts nothing. The host's declared capacity is the vCPU and MemTotal join measured, measured again at every start of serve. A task past that capacity with what the runner holds is put back and held back a moment, without pausing the runner; one past the whole host goes round the pool until a runner with room takes it.

Only two kinds of payload pass through the control plane:

  • A one-shot artifact is served through the API rather than redirected to, because a redirect cannot be counted.
  • Sharding a fan_out: item, pairing a zip, keying a join or evaluating an expression over item needs the items, so the controller reads a step's published envelopes as it decides and retains none. That costs at most envelope_max_bytes per port per step (4 MiB by default), never the artifacts: a hundred gigabyte file travels as a digest and a URI, from runner to runner.

An installation that attaches no object store carries every object through the API as well, since the API is then its object store.

Configuration

Both installations in Install a server set these for you: in compose.yaml, from the AGENTIIK_* variables of its .env, where AGENTIIK_OPERATOR_TOKEN is the one required line (from v0.3.0 the bootstrap token, ignored once it has ended), or in $(brew --prefix)/etc/agentiik. Every one is read at every start, so a setting changed is applied at the next one.

Every program reads AGK_* environment variables. Below, api is agentiik-api serve, controller is agentiik-controller and migrate is agentiik-api migrate, and each reads its own rows and nothing else; agentiik-api init reads the rows naming init. agentiik-api namespace reads AGK_DATABASE_URL and AGK_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE alone, and agentiik-api recover those two and the public URL, AGK_PROXY_URL or AGK_PUBLIC_URL, as the API reads it, so that each runs in the API's own environment with nothing set for it alone. agentiik-api bus-init, bus-credential and audit-verify read no environment: each takes a directory or a file as its one argument, since a person runs it by hand. A server program's secret is never a value: it sits in a file an AGK_*_FILE variable names, since every process the program starts inherits its environment and anybody who can inspect it reads it. The runner keeps its secrets out of the environment another way, in files that join and rotation write for it, listed last below. A variable set to nothing is unset. Durations are written as Go writes them, 90m or 720h: the units stop at hours, and no time at all is refused.

A required setting that is missing, or any setting that is unreadable or malformed, refuses the start and names the variable: a server that started anyway would fail on the first request needing it, and one that fell back to a default would run an installation nobody configured. Every such setting is named on the same start, and a refusal never repeats a value that may hold a secret, whether a URL or the path an _FILE variable holds.

SettingRead byDefaultWhy
Every server program
every AGK_*_FILEits programsas its row saysAn absolute path to a regular file or a link to one, with no permission for its group or anybody else (chmod 600), neither empty nor over 64 KiB: a secret anybody on the host can read is one anybody on the host has, and a refusal is read where a warning is not. AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE is excepted from the mode, as its row says.
AGK_DATABASE_PASSWORD, AGK_MIGRATE_DATABASE_PASSWORD, AGK_BUS_CREDENTIALS, AGK_BUS_ACCOUNT_SEED, AGK_PRESIGN_KEY, AGK_MASTER_KEY, AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN, AGK_METRICS_TOKEN, AGK_AUDIT_EXPORT_TOKEN, AGK_TLS_KEYapi, controller, migrate, initrefusedA secret passed as a value, refused by every program whether or not it reads that secret: write it to a file, and name that file in the variable of the same name ending _FILE. init and migrate take AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN, which has no file, as its row says; every other program refuses it, having no use for it.
PGPASSWORD, PGSSLPASSWORDapi, controller, migraterefusedpgx would sign in, or unlock the client key, with a secret nothing here read. The password goes in AGK_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE; the client key stays unencrypted in a file its owner alone can read, which the URL's sslkey names.
The server programs
AGK_LISTENapi:8080A host and a numeric port, served in plain HTTP to a TLS terminator on a network only it reaches (What every profile must provide), or in TLS by the API itself where AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE names a certificate. 8080 is the port an unprivileged service takes.
AGK_TLS_CERT_FILEapi, controllernone: plain HTTP to a terminator in frontA PEM chain, the server's own certificate first, and no private key: the API serves AGK_LISTEN with it, the controller AGK_METRICS_LISTEN. Held to every AGK_*_FILE rule but the mode, since anybody who connects is sent it. Refused without AGK_TLS_KEY_FILE, expired or not yet valid, and for a controller without AGK_METRICS_LISTEN. TLS 1.2 as the floor, 1.3 where the client speaks it, HTTP/1.1. Read once at start, so a renewed certificate is served from the next restart.
AGK_TLS_KEY_FILEapi, controllernone; required where AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE is setThat certificate's private key, unencrypted PEM, in a file its owner alone can read. Refused without AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE, or where it is not the key of the chain's first certificate.
AGK_PUBLIC_URLapirequired, unless AGK_PROXY_URL is setAn https URL with a host and no user, query or fragment, kept without its trailing slashes: every presigned URL is minted on it, never on a request's Host, and nothing reaches the API in plaintext.
AGK_PROXY_URLapinone: the API is reached at AGK_PUBLIC_URLThe https URL of a proxy on this host that terminates TLS in front of the API, held to AGK_PUBLIC_URL's rules. Set, it is the public URL, and the API serves plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 at AGK_LISTEN's port; AGK_LISTEN naming another host is refused, since the hop without TLS is only safe where no network carries it. AGK_PUBLIC_URL and the TLS pair are then left unread rather than refused, so that one Compose environment serves both ways and setting this one variable chooses. The API then takes a sign-in's address from the last entry of X-Forwarded-For, which the proxy writes, and from nowhere else (Behind a reverse proxy).
AGK_DATABASE_URLapi, controller, migrate, initrequiredA postgres:// URL naming the role the API and the controller connect as, which migrate creates, and carrying no password. From v0.3.0 migrate then signs in as it to keep the bootstrap token's hash, as init does, since the privileged role is for the schema and nothing else. Its sslmode is verify-full, verify-ca or require unless every host is a local socket, because pgx's default, prefer, falls back to plaintext without a word.
AGK_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILEapi, controller, migratenone: the role signs in with a client certificate the URL names, or over a local socketThat role's password, on one line. Refused by init, which generates that password and writes it where the API and the controller read it.
AGK_MIGRATE_DATABASE_URLmigrate, initrequired thereA role that may change the schema, which the application role may not, under the same rules but for naming a role.
AGK_MIGRATE_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILEmigrate, initnoneThat role's password, on one line.
AGK_BUS_URLapi, controllerrequiredOne or more tls:// or wss:// addresses separated by commas, with no user or token: the bus is never reached in plaintext, and every runner is handed this address too.
AGK_BUS_CREDENTIALS_FILEapi, controllerrequiredThe control plane's NATS user credential, its JWT and seed as nsc writes them, valid 90 days. agentiik-api init keeps it in the bus directory of AGK_INIT_DIR, mounted read and write in the API and read only in the controller, so the controller never mounts the directory holding the master key or the account seed. The API looks at it at start and daily, renews it there with the account seed from 14 days before its expiry, and renews one that expired while it was down before starting. The API and the controller reread the file at every connection, so the renewed one is taken with no restart. Where the API cannot renew it, it says why and warns daily. It is refused once expired, since the bus would refuse it; at expiry the controller ends unless the file holds a later one, so nothing is dispatched; the API goes on minting runners' bus credentials, so runners keep the bus and finish what they hold, but creates no runner pool (503).
AGK_BUS_ACCOUNT_SEED_FILEapirequiredThe NATS account seed the API mints runners' short-lived bus credentials with: the account.seed agentiik-api bus-init writes, in a directory kept chmod 700. A seed that is not an account's is refused, since no bus trusts what it signs.
AGK_OBJECTS_DIRapi, controller, and migrate from v0.3.0required by api and controller; none for migrateAn absolute path to an existing directory the program can write in: the built-in object store, until MinIO and S3 (v0.9.0). The API writes objects to it; the controller reads envelopes from it, writes task inputs to it, and, while it leads, deletes from it what the purges and the collection let go of and walks it for files no row names. migrate, run with the API's settings, reads it where it is set, to record the artifact files of the runs v0.2 finished from their envelopes, and asks only to read it, since it writes nothing there and may run where the store is mounted read only; unset, it records none and says so, and the controller records them. The images run as uid 65532 and hold /var/lib/agentiik/objects owned by it, so a volume mounted there is writable.
AGK_PRESIGN_KEY_FILEapirequiredA key of 32 bytes or more in base64, as openssl rand -base64 32 writes one. It signs every presigned URL and upload policy, and every API of an installation holds the same one.
AGK_MASTER_KEY_FILEapirequired; set for the controller, it refuses the controller's startThe key the built-in secret store seals every value under. The sealed values sit in the database the controller shares, so the key, held by the API alone, is what keeps them from it (Secrets).
AGK_ENV_PREFIXESapinone: no namespace may use envnamespace=prefix pairs separated by commas, such as finance=AGK_DEV_FINANCE_: the namespaces opted in to the development-only env provider (Secrets).
AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN_FILEapi until v0.3.0, then migraterequired until v0.3.0, then noneThe SHA-256 of the v0.2 operator token in 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters, never the token, which would be a working credential at rest. From v0.3.0 the API reads the bootstrap token's hash from the database, and migrate alone reads this file, once: where no AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN is set, the database keeps no hash and the bootstrap has not ended, it imports the hash, read as v0.2's API read it, and never reads the file again, so that an installation running no init keeps its token through the upgrade. A file that is not there imports nothing, since an installation made from v0.3.0 may name one it never wrote; one in another shape, or that its group or anybody else may read, fails migrate, naming the variable and never the path. The API, the controller and init pass the variable over, whatever it names, since a v0.2 compose.yaml still sets it (First run).
AGK_MAX_REQUEUEScontroller3max_requeues, a whole number where 0 requeues nothing: the installation's bound on losses (Task states).
AGK_TASK_CEILINGapi, controller1hThe deadline of a step that writes none (Workflow language, Deadlines). The API reads it as the revocation grace's default, so both programs are given the same value.
AGK_JOIN_ROTATIONapi720hHow long a runner credential is accepted for, and how far each rotation moves rotate_by: a machine dark for a month should be reconsidered, not readmitted.
AGK_REVOCATION_GRACEapiAGK_TASK_CEILINGrevocation_grace: how long a revoked runner's results are still taken. A task running past it is declared lost, so an installation whose steps write a longer timeout raises it (Registering a runner). Also bounds every runner bus credential, since a NATS credential runs out rather than being revoked: a grace under an hour means more frequent renewal.
AGK_AUDIT_EXPORT_URLcontrollernone: the log stays in the database, and the controller warns at every startAn https URL with a host and no user: the sink the audit log is exported to, outside the installation (Audit log). A sink behind a private authority is trusted through SSL_CERT_FILE.
AGK_AUDIT_EXPORT_TOKEN_FILEcontrollernone: no Authorization headerThe bearer token the sink wants. Refused without AGK_AUDIT_EXPORT_URL.
AGK_METRICS_LISTENcontrollernone: no metrics, and no portA host and a numeric port the metrics are answered on (Metrics), apart from anything else, since they name every tenant's namespaces and workflows. An address the controller cannot listen on refuses its start. Served in plain HTTP, or over TLS where AGK_TLS_CERT_FILE names a certificate.
AGK_METRICS_TOKEN_FILEcontrollerrequired where AGK_METRICS_LISTEN is set, refused where it is notThe SHA-256 of the token a scrape bears, in 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters, never the token. Prometheus holds the token in its authorization.credentials_file.
AGK_OTLP_ENDPOINTcontrollernone: nothing is tracedThe trace collector, spans posted to /v1/traces below it as OTLP/HTTP JSON, read as OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is (Traces). https, or http to a loopback address alone, with no user, query or fragment; a redirect is refused.
agentiik-api init
AGK_INIT_DIRinitrequiredAn absolute path to a directory whose subdirectories api, controller, nats, bus, runner and objects are the directories each service mounts: each is given its own copy of what it reads, so the controller never mounts the master key and the runner nothing of the control plane's but the certificate. From v0.3.0 init also reads, in objects, the envelopes of the runs v0.2 finished, to record the artifact files they name.
AGK_INIT_HOSTinitrequiredA DNS name or an IPv4 address, with no scheme and no port: the name runners reach the bus at, and clients the API where no proxy is in front, which the certificate is issued to. Changed, init issues the certificate again.
AGK_INIT_NAMESPACEinitrequiredThe namespace init creates, where workflows are pushed and run, held to what the API holds a namespace name to. A previous one stays. It is created at every run where it is missing, since .env names it, so one removed while the line stays comes back at the next start; with no owner, as agentiik-api namespace create makes one. Where a user's login holds the name, which logins and namespace names share, init says so at every run and goes on without it: the installation is no less ready, and every service waits on init.
AGK_OPERATOR_TOKENinit, and migrate from v0.3.0none: the stored hash is kept. Until v0.3.0, init makes a token and prints it once where none was stored; from v0.3.0 neither prints one, and with none set and none stored each says that nobody can create the first administrator. The compose.yaml of agentiik/deploy refuses to start without AGENTIIK_OPERATOR_TOKEN, and from v0.3.0 Homebrew's agentiik-setup writes it to operator-token.env.The one secret taken as a value, since a person writes it once in the file Docker Compose reads, or in Homebrew's settings; init and migrate write its SHA-256 alone, so the plaintext never reaches a disk they write. 32 characters or more, of those a bearer token may hold. Every other program refuses it. From v0.3.0 it is the bootstrap token, whose SHA-256 goes to the database's bootstrap table rather than a file, so that the hash and the token's end are one row the API reads. migrate takes it too, because Homebrew's server and one built by hand run migrate at every start where a Compose file runs init. A changed token replaces the hash at the next run; once the bootstrap token has ended, neither writes anything for it, and each says at every run that the line is ignored (First run).
The runner
AGK_APIagk-runnerrequired; join writes itThe one address a runner is given; the API hands out the rest. https, or http to a loopback address alone, with no user, query or fragment: every call carries the runner's credential.
AGK_RUNNER_LABELSagk-runneroptional; join writes it where the runner claims labelsClaimed at join, within what the token permits; none is a runner of the pool default.
AGK_RUNNER_CONCURRENCYagk-runnerone task per vCPUWhere Sizing says to start. At most 4096, the most keys a heartbeat may name.
AGK_RUNNER_WORKDIRagk-runner/var/lib/agentiik/workAn absolute path: task directories, the record of keys, the trees laid out for tasks (.trees, private to the agent) and the results the bus has not taken with the dispatches a result is owed to (.results, private to the agent: the directory 0700, each file 0600), on the fast disk and writable under ProtectSystem=strict. Join declares the disk available on its filesystem.
AGK_RUNNER_NAMESPACESagk-runnerempty: every namespace the pool acceptsNarrows one host, sent at join and written to runner.env by it (Runner).
AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKENagk-runner servenone: serve does not joinA join token serve joins with where it has to (Registering a runner). Taken as a value, unlike a server program's secret, because it is spent by its one join and refused ever after. Refused beside AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKEN_FILE, since a runner given two would be guessing which was meant.
AGK_RUNNER_JOIN_TOKEN_FILEagk-runner servenoneThe file a join token is in, held to every AGK_*_FILE rule: /etc/agentiik/join-token in the single-host Compose file, which init writes at every run.
DOCKER_HOSTagk-runnerthe local daemon's socketThe daemon the runner drives, as Docker's own clients read it: unix:// or a path. Anything else, tcp:// included, refuses the start of serve and join and names the variable, since a runner drives the daemon on its own host over its local socket alone (Channels).
The runner's files: what join and rotation write, and the helper
/var/lib/agentiik/runner.keyagk-runnerwritten by join, mode 0600The host's Ed25519 key, which signs each rotation and never leaves the machine (Registering a runner).
/etc/agentiik/runner.envagk-runnerwritten by join, mode 0600What join wrote, owned by the agent's account: the credential join returned, beside AGK_API, read by serve itself rather than loaded into its environment. Also where the settings above may be written, in either runner form, and join keeps them; one set in both places with two values refuses the start, trailing slashes on the address and the order of a list aside; given a join token, serve joins again instead of refusing. Read as KEY=VALUE exactly: no quotes, escapes, $, backquotes, export or trailing comments, since a systemd EnvironmentFile= or a Compose env_file would read them differently. Refused as a symbolic link, owned by another account, or readable by its group or others.
AGK_RUNNER_ID, AGK_RUNNER_POOL, AGK_RUNNER_CREDENTIALagk-runnerwritten by join into runner.envThe identifier and the pool the join answered, and the credential. Refused in the environment: the identity is read from the file alone, and a credential in the environment is inherited by every process the agent starts.
/var/lib/agentiik/credentialagk-runnerwritten at the agent's first startThe rotated credential, preferred to runner.env, since the unit's ProtectSystem=strict leaves /etc/agentiik read-only to the agent.
/usr/local/lib/agentiik/agk-helperagk-runnerinstalled beside it, and in the imageThe static helper, bound read-only at /agk/bin/agk for a script step when runner.toml names no helper, from its copy at <work root>/.bin/agk. None installed, or a work root mounted noexec, binds none; a directory there refuses the start.

The host's own settings are in /etc/agentiik/runner.toml (Runner), read at every start of serve. A missing file keeps every default. A key this runner does not read, one spelled otherwise than below, a setting written below a table's header, where TOML makes it a key of that table, and a value outside what its row allows each refuse the start, naming the line: a misspelled setting would otherwise leave its default in force without a word.

KeyDefaultMeaning
require_userns_remaptrueRefuses a daemon without user-namespace remapping; false lifts the floor on this host (Installing a runner). The one floor a line lifts: seccomp and images by digest are held whatever the file says.
secrets_dirnoneRead and unused since v0.2.4: a task's secret values are on a tmpfs volume of its own, which the daemon mounts from memory, so the line can go, and so can the tmpfs it named once nothing is left in it. The runner says so once at start.
stop_grace"10s", the daemon's ownWhole seconds between SIGTERM and SIGKILL, handed to the daemon's stop so that the escalation survives the agent.
helperthe installed /usr/local/lib/agentiik/agk-helper, from its copy under the work rootAn absolute path to the static helper bound read-only at /agk/bin/agk for a script step, used as written; in the container form it is at the same path in the agent's container and on the host. It also fills a task's secrets volume, so a runner with none refuses a task given a secret.
seccomp_profilenone: the daemon's default profileThe absolute path of a JSON profile, read once at start and sent with every create. One that cannot be read, is not a profile, names an action seccomp does not have, or lets every call through refuses the start.
apparmor_profilenone: the daemon's defaultThe name of a profile loaded on the host; unconfined is refused.
selinux_labelnone: the daemon's defaultOne label option, user, role, type, level or filetype, a colon and a value, such as "level:s0:c100,c200". disable and the types the policy leaves unconfined (spc_t, unconfined_t, container_runtime_t) are refused.
allow_cap_addnoneCapability names in capitals without CAP_, such as ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]: all CapAdd may ever carry (Settings applied to every container).
pids_limit256PidsLimit for a step whose resources.pids says nothing, and its ceiling. nproc follows it unless [ulimits] sets it.
memory_capnoneAt least 6Mi, the daemon's floor, with a binary suffix, such as "8Gi": this host's ceiling on Memory, and what a step asking for none gets.
cpu_capnoneCores, at least 0.01, such as "4" or "0.5": this host's ceiling on NanoCPUs, and what a step asking for none gets. More cores than the daemon has refuses the start.
tmp_size"64Mi"The size of the /tmp tmpfs, whose pages are host memory.
log_max_bytes4194304, 4 MiBThe cap on a task's log, standard error alone (Observability).
log_max_lines50000The same cap in lines.
[ulimits] nofile{ soft = 1024, hard = 4096 }Both halves, since the daemon applies them as a pair; hard no lower than soft and at most 1048576, the kernel's default fs.nr_open.
[ulimits] nproc{ soft = 256, hard = 256 }, or pids_limit for bothBoth halves; hard no lower than soft.
[hooks]nonetimeout, pre_task and post_task (Runner-side hooks), held to those three keys and run from v0.9.0; until then the runner says at start that none of them runs.

The bus identity

The bus trusts one operator, created once by agentiik-api bus-init DIR, which signs two accounts: agentiik, with JetStream, and SYS, the system account. It writes three files, each mode 0600, and refuses a directory that already holds any of them.

FileHeld byIs
accounts.confnats-serverThe operator and both accounts, included by the server's own configuration beside its listen address, its TLS certificates and a jetstream block. Nothing secret.
account.seedapiAGK_BUS_ACCOUNT_SEED_FILE
control-plane.credsapi, controllerAGK_BUS_CREDENTIALS_FILE, valid 90 days
Decision

The operator's seed and the system account's are kept nowhere, since nothing signs with either after bus-init and a kept key could sign an account any day.

An installation that needs new accounts creates a new identity in a new directory, restarts the server on it and hands the API and the controller their new files; every runner is given a credential under the new account the next time it asks.

First run

From v0.3.0, an installation starts with no user and one bootstrap token, whose one lasting use is to create the first human administrator:

the first administrator, from v0.3.0
$ export AGENTIIK_TOKEN="$(sed -n 's/^AGENTIIK_OPERATOR_TOKEN=//p' .env)"   # the bootstrap token
$ agk user create alice --admin
alice is an administrator with no credential yet. Open this link once, before 10:15 UTC, to enrol a passkey, or a password where the installation allows one:
https://agentiik.example.com/auth/enrol#<code>
the bootstrap token works until alice has enrolled; then sign in as alice with agk login
StepWhat happens
the bootstrap tokenAGENTIIK_OPERATOR_TOKEN in .env, the v0.2 operator token under its old name; with Homebrew, AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN in operator-token.env, which agentiik-setup writes. init, or migrate where no init runs, keeps its SHA-256 alone, in the database, and no server program prints it or writes it to a log.
agk user create LOGIN --adminRun with the bootstrap token, it creates the administrator and answers an enrolment link, shown once: single use, good for an hour. Run again for the same login before it has enrolled, as POST /api/v1/users/{login}/enrolment is, it answers a fresh link and revokes the one before, so a link that lapsed unused locks nobody out.
the linkOpens the API's enrolment page, which runs the passkey ceremony and records the account's first credential, or, where the policy allows passwords, as it always does on an installation addressed by an IP address, sets a password instead.
the token endsThe token ends once an administrator it created, not suspended, can sign in to a full session: at their first passkey, however it is registered, and at a password, set from a code or signed in with, that opens a full session, as on an installation addressed by an IP address or wherever the policy requires no passkey. A password set where a passkey is required opens a session that only enrols, and the token goes on until the first passkey registered from it. The end invalidates the bootstrap token, forgets its hash and revokes any other first administrator's link still open; the recovery codes it issued open nothing from then on; and the audit log records bootstrap.end. The line stays in .env, which compose.yaml still requires; init, or migrate, says at every run that it is ignored, which is not an error, and never writes a hash for it again, so that no token can start the bootstrap over. A run the bootstrap token started that has not been let in by then ends cancelled, naming the end; one already running goes on.
thenThe administrator creates namespaces, each with its owner, groups and users. An owner of a namespace creates its service accounts and mints their tokens, agk service-account create finance/ci then agk token create --for finance/ci, and a script that used the bootstrap token holds such a token instead. Every user gets a personal namespace on first sign-in.
Until v0.3.0

A v0.2 installation has no principals, so it has one operator: a token whose hash sits in the file AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN_FILE names. agentiik-api identifies it as one principal allowed every permission at every scope, and everyone else stays denied. From v0.3.0 the same token is the bootstrap token, whose hash init, or migrate where no init runs, keeps in the database, migrate importing it once from that file: after an upgrade the API takes it as a bootstrap principal, an administrator owning every namespace, so it does what it did and the runs recorded as triggered_by: operator stay readable, until it ends.

Decision

The bootstrap token is the operator token rather than a new one, because an upgrade changes compose.yaml and .env and nothing else, and a new token would have to be read from a log, which is copied, shipped and kept by more people than .env. It ends when the first administrator can sign in to administer, not at their creation, because until then the token is the only way in, and a link that lapsed would otherwise leave an installation nobody can administer; nor at a password set where the policy requires a passkey, since that password opens a session that only enrols. It ends then because a secret that may do everything, shared by whoever reads one file, is what principals replace: a service account's token has a namespace, an expiry and a revocation of its own.

agentiik-api init does all of this in the Compose installation, at every start. In Homebrew, agentiik-setup does it once and, from v0.3.0, the service runs agentiik-api migrate at every start, which keeps the bootstrap token's hash as init does. Below is the same for an installation put together by hand, from v0.3.0.

by hand, the first time, from v0.3.0
# the bootstrap token: keep it, and give migrate alone the token itself
$ token=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
$ AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN=$token agentiik-api migrate   # keeps its hash in the database
$ agentiik-api namespace create finance
$ agentiik-api bus-init /var/lib/agentiik/bus     # then start nats-server on accounts.conf

$ agentiik-api serve                               # without the token, which it refuses; agentiik-controller beside it
$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $token" https://agentiik.example.com/api/v1/runner-pools
{"runner_pools":[{"pool":{"name":"default","labels":[],"namespaces":[],"resource_ceilings":{},"containment":"hardened"}}]}

# on the runner host, as root, with a join token of default
$ agk-runner join --api https://agentiik.example.com --token <token of default>

Run again without AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN, migrate keeps the stored hash; with another token, it replaces it, until the bootstrap token has ended. The namespace agentiik-api namespace create makes has no owner, as one made by v0.2 has none, and the first runner joins the pool default claiming no label. A run the bootstrap token starts records triggered_by: operator.

Until v0.3.0 the API read the hash from a file instead: what printf %s "$token" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1 writes, the token hashed without a trailing newline, in a file of mode 0600 that AGK_OPERATOR_TOKEN_FILE names. An installation put together that way upgrades by running the new release's migrate before serve, with the settings it already has: migrate imports that hash once, where the database keeps none, and the token it was made with goes on working as the bootstrap token; given the API's AGK_OBJECTS_DIR, it also records the artifact files v0.2 left unrecorded, which the controller records otherwise. serve passes the variable over, so no setting has to change.

Push notification delivery

For mobile alerts, an installation gives the API its own APNs key and Firebase service account. Both are optional: without them there is no push, and the applications poll in the foreground.

§

Repositories

Thirteen repositories in the agentiik organisation, split by what has to be released together, not by language.

RepositoryContentsStack
agentiik/agentiikThe core, as one module: graph evaluator, container driver, controller, HTTP API, runner and the agk command line. One module keeps the evaluator and the driver importable libraries, so agk run --local is the same code path as a server run.Go
agentiik/schemasJSON Schema 2020-12 for the workflow file, the brick manifest and the envelope, plus the OpenAPI document. A keyword without description and examples fails the build, because the site's language reference and workflow.language are generated from here.JSON, YAML
agentiik/bricksThe standard catalog, one directory per brick (image, manifest, example envelopes), built and published as one matrix.mixed
agentiik/brick-sdkOptional envelope helpers for Go, Python and TypeScript. The contract stands without them.mixed
